speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 337, to amend the criminal code.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO DEFAMATORY LIBEL, CULPABLE HOMICIDE, ETC.
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO DEFAMATORY LIBEL, CULPABLE HOMICIDE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill contains forty-six sections, some of them merely correcting errors, some of them improving language, it is hoped, and some of them making relatively unimportant changes in procedure. There are, however, at least half a dozen sections of considerable importance. One is the section providing that the rules relating to place of trial of a defamatory libel published in a newspaper are to be made applicable to the place of trial of a conspiracy to publish a defamatory libel. Another provision is to the effect that the term "culpable homicide", instead of including as at present only murder and manslaughter, is to include a third offence to be known as "infanticide".
Another provision is that there shall be a minimum penalty of one year's imprisonment for stealing from the mails. Then there are amendments to prevent the fraudulent manipulation of transactions on stock exchanges, and otherwise to facilitate the curbing of security frauds.
Part XVI of the code is completely withdrawn and changed in important respects. The changes are so important that it would not be prudent to bring the new part XVI into force
on the passing of the act, and therefore it is proposed that it come into force on the first day of October, 1949. The reasons for that postponement will appear when the bill is discussed.
Provision is made for a jury trial continuing by consent of both the crown and the accused, even though one or two jurors, through illness or other causes, are unable to continue to act.
Provision is made for indeterminate sentences of not less than two years upon the trial of persons charged with certain sex offences, if these persons are found to be criminal sexual psychopaths.
These, I think, are the most important amendments. Perhaps there are other amendments which will strike some hon. members as having considerable importance, and which can be discussed at a later stage.
I should like to say also that no attempt has been made to amend the gambling sections, although we have had strong representations, particularly from the attorney general's department of the province of Ontario, in favour of so doing. It would be idle for me to deny that the gambling sections need amending, but the only province that has made definite and comprehensive proposals for amendment is Ontario. In a matter of this importance it was finally decided that the suggestions of the attorney general's department of the province of Ontario, together with the modifications of these suggestions suggested by the Department of Justice, should be laid before the commissioners on the uniformity of legislation, criminal side, next August for their consideration so that the views of all the departments of the attorneys general in Canada might be obtained before amendments are introduced. It is realized that this delay will be a disappointment to the department of the attorney general of Ontario, but, on the whole, it seemed to be the wisest course to take in the circumstances.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-DAMAGE TO TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY LINES
speechtext: Mr. ' Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. I sent him notice of it on Friday last. Can he make a statement as to the probable extent of the damage to the trans-continental railway lines through British Columbia, and when it is expected that rail communication will be reestablished with the Pacific coast?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-DAMAGE TO TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am able to make a statement concerning the two railways, the present condition of their lines, and the extent of damage to each.
The management of the Canadian National Railways inform me that on the line to Vancouver communication has been re-established as far west as Boston Bar. The expectation is that emergency restoration on the line as far west as Hope will be completed by June 10. Intermediate communication is being established at Hope in the expectation that emergency restoration from Hope to Chilliwack will be completed by June 8. Thus, by the combination of forces working concurrently west from Boston Bar and west and east from Hope, it is expected that communication as far west as Chilliwack will be completed by June 10. The line beyond Chilliwack to Port Mann is still inundated, and it is quite impossible to forecast the extent of damage in this section and the probable date of restoration of the line.
On the Prince Rupert line, Canadian National communication will be re-established as far as Tatlow, which is six miles east of Smithers, by tomorrow. With restoration of damage at Tatlow by about June 10, the line will be open as far west as Kitwanga, which is seventy-three miles west of Smithers. Concurrently, working crews from Prince Rupert have reached Salvus, sixty-five miles to the east. The condition of the section from Kitwanga to Salvus is still indeterminate, especially

Excise Tax Act
*because of conditions immediately west of Kitwanga which appear to be serious. More definite predictions as to the reopening of the line through to Prince Rupert will depend on more detailed inspection and the more authentic information as to conditions between Kitwanga and Salvus. It is not possible at this time to estimate the cost of restoration work, but we know it will be heavy and will probably involve several millions of dollars.
I am advised by the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway that they are hopeful of having, and expect to have, a complete line to Vancouver by June 15, with a complete restoration of service shortly thereafter. The line from Calgary to Hope is expected to be open any time now', and if the highway from Hope to Vancouver is opened to traffic, it would then be possible to transfer passengers and their baggage from railway to buses at that point, thus providing a combination rail-highway service from Calgary to Vancouver early this w'eek. The company at this time, without having received full engineering estimates with respect to certain parts of their line which are still badly inundated, estimate that the cost of rehabilitation of their lines in the British Columbia region will amount to slightly less than $1,000,000.
In conversation with the Canadian National this morning I was advised that their line is open as far as Kamloops from which point traffic is detoured to the Canadian Pacific line as far as Hope. Passengers, mail and express are then moved by highway from Hope to Vancouver. Yesterday the Canadian National transferred to highway services nine carloads of emergency food and supplies for Vancouver destination.
Both railways are endeavouring to ascertain that the Great Northern is in a position to handle Vancouver traffic before issuing instructions to reroute all of this traffic over the Great Northern.
Just before I came into the house I spoke to officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway, who report that 50 carloads of freight, including foodstuffs, have already been rerouted via the Great Northern to Vancouver. It is expected it will take seven days to reach its destination.

speechtext:
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 332, to amend the Excise Tax Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Mutch in the chair.
On section 1-"Minister".

Not having had anything to say on the budget, because I was absent when the matter was before the house, I w'ish to ascertain the minister's views on one question to which I shall refer now.
A major source of criticism on the part of the people at all times has to do with payment of taxes, and at the present time their complaints are certainly not unjustified. I realize, as the minister said in his budget speech, that the larger proportion of government expenditures consists of uncontrollable items. Social security items amount to 16-25 per cent of the total budget; veterans' pensions, 14-85 per cent; national defence, 8-87 per cent; interest and carrying charges on the national debt, 21-21 per cent. I feel that the time has come for the assumption by parliament of responsibility for the careful examination of expenditures. The suggestion has been made before, but in general terms. As I see the expansion of government expenditures from year to year, it occurs to me that the policy of the government is to spend and spend, and to tax and tax. Parliament has not taken a strong stand against over-expenditures; the result is the present situation.
If you look at Hansard over the last twenty-five years, Mr. Chairman, you will find that immediately before and after the first world war there was on the part of the House of Commons a definite desire to reduce expenditures and definite activity in the challenging of items that might be reduced; whereas in recent years parliament in the last two or three weeks of the session has passed innumerable items running into millions and tens of millions, without any examination whatsoever on the part of the house.
Throughout the country there is strong resentment against parliament because of its failure to reduce expenditures recommended by the government; for unless there is reduction in expenditure there will not be reduction in taxation. A number of years ago Sir George Foster, one of the most outstanding parliamentarians of 'his time-and his viewpoint was subsequently reinforced by an independent research investigation-suggested that there be set up a special house committee on estimates. Today we find ourselves in the position of making general attacks on every expenditure. Regardless of economic experimentation by theorists who advise the government, parliament accepts their suggestions and does little toward endeavouring to reduce expenditures. Two years ago Mr. Watson Sellar, the auditor general, asked for the setting up of special committees to comb the estimates-and I direct
Excise Tax Act

attention to the word "comb"-before they are submitted to the house as a whole. I ask the minister if such a committee would not be helpful. The other day he told us that the treasury board discharges that responsibility. Indeed, if I remember aright what he said, he actually told the treasury board that only they would in the end determine the extent of expenditures and the economies that could be effected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not tell treasury board that. I told the various departmental officials coming in with their estimates.

Yes. That statement, made the other day, impressed me, indicating as it does that the House of Commons is not discharging its responsibilities. Here we have a statement by the Minister of Finance, after a year's experience in office, that the heads of departments alone act as a deterrent against over-expenditure, and that upon them alone it depends.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not upon them; treasury board is the only one that really scrutinizes the items.

I am not playing with words. I am stating in substance what the minister has placed before the house. I ask him whether consideration has been given to Mr. Sellar's suggestion and if so, why it has not been carried beyond consideration. Why should members of this house not be divided into committees, as suggested by Mr. Sellar, to the end that expenditures shall be reduced where they ought to be reduced. Unless something is done, there will be no improvement. If the heads of departments, as a result of the failure of the House of Commons to challenge the estimates, are unable to resist the demands made upon them, they are given an incentive to increase expenditures; they realize that the house as a whole will not challenge their recommendations to treasury board, which recommendations are passed on to the house.
On a previous occasion, when mention was made of a suggestion not the same as this, the minister passed it off in a manner which, while it could not be described as flippant, did not do justice to the seriousness of the problem. To continue to tax and tax- with the load that today rests on the person in the low-income brackets, caught as he is between the rising cost of living, about which little or nothing has been done by the government, and an income little increased since the end of the war-is a policy against which resentment is generally felt. We in this house should do our part to be of assistance 
to the minister in reducing unnecessary expenditures and preventing administrative officials from joining in what finally becomes an orgy of over-expenditure unless departmental officials and others feel that their estimates will be challenged by the house as a whole.
This is not a new suggestion. It was made as far back as 1910, when expenditures totalled about $100,000,000. Today, with expenditures amounting to many times that total, the necessity of some such action is even more apparent. In reading Hansard for those days, as no doubt the minister has, one is particularly struck by the fact that then, and indeed until about 1925 or 1926, the House of Commons as a whole in committee seemed to be seized of its responsibility toward the people to pare down if possible and challenge where necessary over-expenditure or over-generous expenditure.
Is the minister prepared to consider the setting up of committees along the lines suggested by Mr. Sellar? If he is, parliament would not have to sit as long, and the house would be discharging its major responsibility, that of acting as watch dog of the treasury. The advantage would pass to the taxpayers in the reduction of controllable expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not want to interrupt my hon. friend, because I know he was not able to be here during the main budget discussion. It is customary to permit general remarks on the first section of a bill, but I think the ordinary rule is that they should relate to the bill in question rather than to broad topics. However, I did not interrupt my hon. friend because I realized that in the circumstances it was desirable for him to make his remarks; but I hope the practice will not be followed by other hon. members, and that my failure to raise any protest will not be treated as acquiescence in a complete revival of the budget discussions.
I should like to reply briefly to one point raised by the hon. member, in connection with the committees he mentioned. I have done so before, I think on an earlier occasion this session. I believe the view I expressed was that the creation of functional committees of the kind is foreign to our parliamentary system. Whether or not that is true, my personal view is that the job of scrutinizing the detailed estimates is one which should not be delegated to a small committee of the house. Traditionally this House of Commons has considered it to be its right to discuss each item of the estimates. As I said before, my own experience has been that discussion does not always relate directly to the item of expenditure which is under consideration, but frequently to general matters

Excise Tax Act
having to do with the department. I may be wrong, of course, but I question very much whether the adoption of the system which has been suggested by Mr. Sellar, high though my respect is for that very capable official, would result in any reduction in expenditure. After four or five years of close association with the Department of Finance I have come to the reluctant conclusion that the only real check on expenditures lies with the Minister of Finance first, and the treasury board second. I hope I am wrong in that, but I do not think I am. Human nature being what it is, I believe the general tendency on the part of members of parliament and a great many others is to be generous with the public money. They know the Minister of Finance has to be tough in these things, and that treasury board has to look pretty carefully at the larger expenditures; and in my not too lengthy experience here I have not heard many suggestions for a reduction in expenditure.
I do not believe the formation of such committees would really produce the result I know we would all desire, the elimination of unnecessary expenditures. I am afraid that is a responsibility which must be assumed primarily by the government, with parliament discharging its traditional responsibility by looking at the items of expenditure and deciding whether or not it wants to approve them.
I point out, too, as I have done before, that the estimates are brought down early in the session, with itemized details showing exactly how it is proposed that the public money be spent. These are before the house for months. It is true that in some respects the formality of passing some of the expenditures item by item is left until late in the session, but that does not mean every member of the House of Commons has not ample opportunity to give careful scrutiny to all proposed expenditures.
I am completely out of order in discussing this matter here, I am afraid; but since my hon. friend brought it up, and since it is a very important question, I felt that I should be permitted to answer his statement.

I should like to add just a few words at this point concerning a matter on which I have said something on two or three previous occasions. The day will come when spending on the basis on which it is now proceeding will come to an end. I do not think there is any doubt about that. At present we are indulging in the experiment of management, and for the time being we are producing that which enables us to spend accordingly; but some day soon a re-establishment of real values will take place. When that day comes, reductions in taxation will have to be made; and I am asking the minister,
as I did the other night, to set up a committee or to cause his officials to study the matter with a view to bringing about reductions without great and irreparable loss. When taxes are imposed on commodities, they are collected and received by the government. When taxes are taken off, however, the purchaser or consumer will not pay them, even though they may have been paid by the manufacturer or importer. I suggest to the minister that it is the part of prudence and justice to examine carefully the procedure which should be followed when war taxes are abandoned, as they must be, in order that their abandonment may not cause grave and unnecessary harm to the people who paid them in the first place and who must recoup themselves or be greatly injured. I would therefore ask the minister to have the question examined by his departmental officials and, if possible, to provide an opportunity to members to assist the government in the study of a measure which is bound to have such far-reaching consequences.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I again point out that there is little use in setting up a committee of the house to revise the rules if we are not prepared to stick as closely as possible to the rules we already have. I submit it is completely out of order to discuss topics relating to general taxation when we have before us section 1 of a bill to amend the Excise Tax Act. I would ask hon. members to co-operate in this regard and to stick to the section. We have had a pretty full discussion on general topics.

When the minister rose I was on the point of saying that this discussion has been of a general nature, and that a general debate on the budget is not in my view permissible in respect of this specific bill. I have desired not to be hasty, but the statement I have made indicates no temerity on my part. Shall section 1 carry?
Mr. DIEFENBAIvER: No. With all due respect, we are discussing taxation. This bill has to do with amendments to a taxing act known as the Excise Tax Act. When the minister talks about getting along, may I point out to him that this year he has got along so fast that a record has been established. I believe that in the last twenty-five years no finance minister has had his budget resolutions considered as quickly as they were this year, having regard to the resentment felt by the people of Canada against high taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Order. Can we not abide by the rules of the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not mind how much time we take, and I was endeavouring to be courteous. However I must insist upon strict enforcement of the rules. The rules with respect to consideration of a bill in committee are quite clear. Discussion must be relevant to the clause before the committee-not the whole bill, but the particular clause. By a sort of tradition, general discussion has been allowed on section 1. But that is only through tolerance; it has no support in the rules; indeed it is an infraction of them. I do not wish to raise any disturbance, but when my hon. friend asks me to be patient I would answer that I have listened without interruption; and I think, you, sir, should enforce the rules.

Let us not get into a discussion about how we are going to proceed. We are anxious to get on with the work, and the best way to get on with it is to proceed in the manner to which we have become accustomed. Discussion of the general terms of a bill has always been allowed on the first section. If the minister would smile, perhaps we would get on faster.

The rule respecting speeches in committee is clear. Throughout this session a serious attempt has been made by the committee of the whole to get back to something more closely resembling the rules than the practice which prevailed during the difficult war years, when general discussion was permitted to a greater extent. As hon. members are aware, I do not ordinarily preside over the committee, and for that reason I hesitated at the beginning to rise or to interrupt, or to have my first words a reference to the rules. The rule, however, is specific in this matter, and if I am required to do so I shall have to rule to enforce it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am usually pretty fair in these matters. In my earlier remarks I appealed to the committee to stick as closely as possible to the rules. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that that question has never been raised departmentally and I am afraid I am not in position to answer it offhand. One of the principal purposes of amending section 10 is to remove the word "war". The new act is to be known as the Excise Tax Act instead of the Excise War Tax Act. In section 115 the reference to the board of customs is deleted, because it was replaced a good many years ago by the tariff board.

I have become accustomed to seeing orders in council take on the power and effect of statutes, but it has never before
come to my attention that an independent irresponsible body named as the tariff board is named has the power to enact legislation which is the law of the land to the same extent as if a bill had been brought into the house, debated, read three times, passed and sent to the senate and finally given the royal assent. Of course I may not be fully informed, but this is a startling provision because it says that a declaration by the tariff board under this section shall have the same force and effect as if it had been sanctioned by statute. I am aware that a declaration by the board of customs had a somewhat similar effect, but the board of customs was a slightly different organization, and I believe there was always an appeal from that board.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course whatever remedies there are would lie here. The board of customs was replaced years ago by the tariff board. As my hon. friend will see on looking at the section, it relates largely to an interpretation of descriptions in the tariff schedule. The tariff board may declare what amount of tax is payable thereon, or that the article is exempt from tax under this act. Before the creation of the tariff board apparently that was the function of the board of customs, which consisted of officials in the government service. For many years past-since 1933 at any rate- the responsibility for performing these functions has been vested in the tariff board. I am informed that this is simply to bring the law into conformity with what has been the practice during those years.

I should like to know how this will work out in a practical way. As I understand it, when there is doubt or dispute with respect to the amount of duty to be paid on any article reference is made to the tariff board, which may in its uncontrolled discretion make a declaration as to the result, when-and I quote from the section:
-there is no previous decision upon the question by any competent tribunal binding throughout Canada.

A deduction from, or refund of, any of the taxes imposed by this act may be granted:
(a) where an overpayment has been made by the taxpayer.
Just as a matter of historical information, may I say I am told that subsection 2, which we are now discussing, has been in the act since 1917. It was put in in 1917 and the only change here is that the tariff board was substituted in 1933, as the hon. member for Stanstead will recall, for the board pf cus-

toms. The tariff board is now the tribunal to decide whether refunds may be made.

I began my question by asking whether there was an appeal. I understood that there was not. I am going to ask the minister to bear with me just a moment while we consider section 115, which reads as follows:
Where any difference arises or where any doubt exists as to whether any or what rate of tax is payable on any article under this act and there is no previous decision upon the question by any competent tribunal binding throughout Canada, the tariff board constituted by the Tariff Board Act may declare what amount of tax is payable thereon or that the article is exempt from tax under this act.
Then follows the section which says that the declaration of the tariff board has the same effect as a statute. What happens when there is a dispute as to whether or not there is a previous decision? My hon. friend, who has spent long years before the courts, knows that sometimes lawyers cannot agree whether a case is pertinent or not, whether it applies or not. Even courts have been known to disagree as to whether or not they are bound by a certain decision. Who is to be the arbiter in these cases? Is the tariff board to determine once and for all, and beyond all possibility of appeal, that a case does not apply, when others, possibly entitled to an opinion equally respectable, feel that it does?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is an interesting question. I have never considered it before, and the senior official of the Department of National Revenue, w'ho is sitting in front of me, tells me it has not come up. My opinion, for what it is worth, would be that the question whether or not there has been a decision by a competent tribunal is a question of fact; and if the tariff board, or any other body, purported to declare that there had not been when in fact there had been, then clearly there would be an appeal from that finding, I would think. But I am talking at odds. It is a question of fact as to whether there has been a decision.
I think it is a question of law. Would the minister not go so far as to say that it is a mixed question of law and of fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may well be.
I want to know' who this competent body is. I asked that a moment ago. Who is the competent body that is going to set this precedent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot answer that question at the moment. The exchequer court is the body which in general deals with all appeals on matters of the kind. As I say,

Excise Tax Act
this section has been in the statute for thirty odd years. Perhaps the question should have been raised before. It was enacted by a government of which my hon. friend was a supporter. The tariff board was substituted for the board of customs in 1933 when my hon. friend's party was in pow'er. There is no change in the law. The same body has the power to declare that it shall have the same force and effect as if it had been sanctioned by statute-that has been in the law for a long time-instead of a board of officials. It is now the tariff board. As to the question whether there is an appeal from that tribunal, I -would have to give it consideration. I am afraid I cannot answer it at the moment. It is an interesting question, and frankly it has caught me by surprise.

The minister says that this provision has been in the statute for a long time. It is illustrative of the removal by administrative bodies of the right of the individual to recourse to the courts in order to protect his rights. The tendency in that direction has been accelerated during the last few years. Up to 1923 there were three or four statutes which denied the individual the right of recourse to the courts. Since then they have been increased in number, to an extent not known in any other of the British dominions. As a matter of fact it was the denial of the right of the individual to recourse to the courts that caused Mr. Justice Angers of the exchequer court to make a protest against the infringement by the executive on the rights of the judiciary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is not an action of the executive.

No, but it is the type of legislation to which Mr. Justice Angers made -reference in these words:
There are, in my judgment, far too many encroachments from ministers, deputy ministers and functionaries in the judicial as well as the legislative field.
In the last few years statute after statute has been enacted which has placed the average citizen in such a position that he may be ordered, directed or pushed around by administrative officials, while at the same time he is denied the right to appeal to a higher authority to protect him from the actions of officialdom. As a matter of fact, the whole essence of the right of appeal is that the intemperate or arbitrary action of the crown, or its officials, shall be reviewed by the courts. This section in its present form simply means that whether a tax applies or not, whether under the law it can properly be applied, when the tariff board
makes its declaration the matter is final, and regardless of the law, that declaration shall have the same force and effect as if sanctioned by statute. That is going a long way. It may have been on the statute book for years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Put on by a Conservative government.

No, put on by a mixture-and by the way, sir, this is the first time I have heard my hon. friend endeavour to get out of his responsibility by saying that what w^e have before us represents in part a statute passed by a Conservative government. Regardless of who put it on, or when, the present government, relying on one or two statutes passed prior to 1922, has accelerated the tendency in that direction. The result is that our statutes are replete with the type of legislation which denies to the individual the right of appeal to the courts that he may obtain the king's justice, that right being withheld regardless of unfairness or of the injustice that is done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I should have pointed out that the taxpayer has the option of appealing to the tariff board or to the courts. He can take his choice. I had always understood that the tariff board was a semijudicial body. If the taxpayer is dissatisfied with the ruling of the departmental officials he can appeal, I am told, to the courts or to the tariff board.

But the alternative is not provided by section 115. "Where any difference arises"

that would be as between the crown and the individual-"or where any doubt exists as to whether any tax is payable on any article under this act," then the tariff board may make its declaration. It not only exercises discretion in determining the rate of tax, which is administrative, but it also has the right to make a judicial declaration as to whether any tax is payable. That section provides two things: first, an administrative right, namely, the determination of the rate of tax payable where dispute takes place-and I can understand such an administrative board so determining; but it also has the judicial power of determining, regardless of the law, whether any tax is payable. In that case the decision is final, regardless of whether parliament ever intended that the item in question should be subjeot to tax.

speechtext: I will have that looked into. I am told that under section 105, which I mentioned, refunds are made every day where taxes are paid in error. If the minister is sure there is appeal-

I am assured by the officer in front of me, who has 'been in the Department of National Revenue for many years and has charge of this division, that that is and has been the practice. The taxpayer, if dissatisfied with the decision of the department, has the option of appealing to the exchequer court or of going to the tariff board. It used to be the board of customs. speechtext: But is for the taxation year, 1946?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right. The similar statistical publication for the current year is now in process of preparation, and will be ready in August or September.
I would ask for the information for the current year.
I should like to refer to the second part of section 3, which refers to charitable bequests. Why was that change made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe it was last year I received a delegation from the various Protestant churches at first, headed by my old friend, Mr. Hamilton Cassels. It was urged that in Quebec and Ontario, where succession duties are still imposed, there had always been complete exemption for charitable bequests, and that this constituted discrimination on the part of the dominion in allowing an exemption for only 50 per cent. I had similar representations from the Roman Catholic church, from heads of universities and others, and I came to the conclusion that the revenue implications were not great. I think I mentioned that it amounted to only $300,000 or $400,000 a year. It seemed to me that our law should conform to the existing provincial law.
Is there any definition of the word "charitable"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, there is not. This has been pretty well established as a result of a long line of cases, principally English cases, going back a good many years. It is pretty well known now what is charitable. I know there has been some discussion in connection with income tax matters as to whether such things as community halls and so on would come within the definition. It is some time since I have looked up the cases, but I understand it has been pretty well established by
Dominion Succession Duty Act

jurisprudence as to what is covered by a charitable bequest.
Mr. HA'ZEN: The legal definition is quite broad and includes a great deal. I think it would include a society for the promulgation of a particular political doctrine or principle, such as socialism or Conservatism-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That last one is charity.
-combined with moral or moral improvement. That is going pretty far.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree if that is the case, but I do not think it is the case.

I understand that a gift to increase the efficiency of the army would be regarded as charitable at law, or a gift providing for the improvement of agriculture; any gift of that kind might be charitable at law and come within the legal definition. It seems to me that the government might be losing revenue it should have if it regards gifts of that kind as charitable and has no restrictive definition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those are some interesting cases put forward by my hon. friend. I am afraid that no attempt has ever been made in any statute to define what is a charitable bequest or a charitable gift. I think this is one of the cases that could best be left to the courts. I am sure the hon. member for Lake Centre will agree with that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the same definition of "charitable" apply in this case as applies to the ordinary annual income tax return?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Exactly the same.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: A very interesting suggestion has been made by the hon, member for St. John-Albert.
I should like the minister to advise me with respect to the interpretation of "institution", such as applying to a school for the blind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would say that it would clearly come under it.

If that is the case in this particular act, would it also apply as far as the sales tax is concerned? A recent inquiry was made by the Halifax school for the blind, which is one of only three schools of its kind in Canada, as to whether or not it could be exempted from the payment of sales tax in connection with food and supplies for its pupils. No favourable decision has as yet been given. I am hoping that in the light of the statement made today by the minister,

his officials will in future be able to exempt this school from the payment of sales tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Excise Tax Act is the statute under which the sales tax is imposed. Exemption from sales tax depends upon the type of institution to which the material is supplied. If it is an institution approved by the Department of National Health and Welfare it would be entitled to sales tax exemption on materials purchased.

Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Since this bill has just been distributed, is there any particular reason for bringing it forward this afternoon? The hon. member who has just spoken said he had not read the bill, and I think that is true of all hon. members. If there is some particular reason for proceeding with it I shall not object.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no particular
reason, and if the committee would prefer I would be glad to hold it over. I would point out that the full content of the bill was printed in the resolution. I have not had an
opportunity of looking at the bill. Is this not the bill concerning which discussion of the resolution was deferred because it purported to change the British preference? On that result it may be well that we should discuss first the Geneva agreements.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, that is another bill
which was put forward the other day in my absence, and my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, agreed that it should be allowed to stand. This bill merely implements the budget resolutions with respect to the tariff changes. It is not the bill to which my hon. friend refers.
What I am anxious to know is this. If we pass this bill, are we not putting an end to the British preference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that is not the case. As a matter of fact, one effect of the amendment which I proposed the other night, when the resolution stage was being considered, maintained the existing tariff rates in regard to this bill, and not the tariff changes proposed under the Geneva agreements. In this bill there is no giving effect to any of the Geneva rates, none whatever.
No other changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The only changes we are proposing here are permanent tariff changes, in so far as any tariff change is permanent.

I recall that at the time of the Ottawa agreements an arrangement was made whereby the preference should work both ways. Canada was given a preference in the British market ; and, as a consideration for that, the preference that Britain had in our market passed out of the jurisdiction of the governor in council and became a matter of rigid law which could not be changed except by parliament. I notice in this bill that there are several references to the British preference. It would be unfortunate if, after passing this bill we found out that we had done something which we did not wish to do. I suggest to the minister that he defer consideration of this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I say a word? I am assured by the commissioner of tariffs, who is sitting in front of me, that there is no such change as that suggested by my hon. friend. The Customs Act, which was before the house the other day, is the act which was deferred. This is the Customs Tariff Act. The changes here are simply changes in rates. It is true that there is one other change. We are using the description ''most favoured nation" for "intermediate" because, in fact, that is what it has been called for a number of years. That is the only change. There is no implementation of the Geneva agreements as a result of these amendments to the customs tariff.

Will the minister look at section 2, which substitutes a new section 4, paragraph (b) of which reads as follows:
Withdraw the benefit of the British preferential tariff, in whole or in part . . .
And so on. I dislike speaking without more opportunity for verifying the accuracy of my recollection, but it is my memory that by the agreements of 1932 we are unable to do exactly what we are purporting to do by this new section 4. paragraph (b). For the reason I suggest to the minister that he afford the committee an opportunity of acquainting itself with the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To clear up that point, may I say that the new section 4 is a repetition of section 4 as it now stands in the customs tariff, but where the words "intermediate tariff" appear in the section we are substituting the words "most favoured nation". That is done throughout the section. It seems simpler to do it in that way than to repeal the section and re-enact it. We could have put in the rather complicated amending technique and say , "By substituting the words 'most favoured nation'
Customs Tariff

for 'intermediate' I give my hon. friend the assurance that that is the only change of substance, if it can be called a change of substance, in the existing section.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I share the concern of the hon. member for Stanstead with respect to the point we came up against the other day in dealing with Bill No. 229. If I thought this bill was asking us to brush off that problem I would support him in asking that consideration of Bill No. 333 be delayed, but I am satisfied that such is not the case. Bill No. 229 has still to come up, and we on this side would like it to wait until the discussion on the Geneva agreements is out of the way. But this bill-Bill No. 333-is clearly just the statutory implementation of the provisions of the budget resolutions with respect to the customs tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There is at least one section in this 'bill with which I do not agree; there may be more, 'but at least it does not take me by surprise. We were given all this information in the course of the discussion on the budget resolutions preceding the customs tariff. I think we would be well advised to go ahead and deal with it today.
Does this bill reduce the tariff on a good many items?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quite a number of items, which I outlined in my budget speech, mostly production items.
Under the Geneva agreements, if we reduce these tariffs we can never put them back again as long as the agreements are in force.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We can put them back up to the rates fixed under the Geneva agreements. I think I answered that the other night. We could not put them above the Geneva agreements. If in some cases here, I cannot answer offhand, we have reduced the rates below those stipulated in the Geneva agreements we can put the rates back up to the levels established under the Geneva agreement rates, assuming we approved them, but we could not go above them.
Have we reduced some below the rates agreed upon by the Geneva agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told that there are a few incidental ones. It was possible to get them down, but they are not very many.
[Mr Abbott.]

Does this mean that if, in fact, the Geneva agreements are not eventually approved we would have taken an action which would limit our future action in respect of them? That is what I took from what the minister said. I took it that we would have limited ourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The action we have taken here does not affect us one way or the other, whether we approve or disapprove the Geneva agreements. If there happened to be tariff changes below the rates stipulated in the Geneva agreements, and we confirmed the Geneva agreements, we could not put them back up again higher than the tariff rates in the Geneva agreements. If the Geneva agreements are not confirmed, our tariff position is exactly the same as it was before the negotiations of the Geneva agreements. We could change our rates up and down as we saw fit.

I understand that, and I do not wish to restate my position. It does seem to me strange that we should take an attitude on these articles in the tariff before we consider the Geneva agreements. My hon. friend has said that he would have brought forth these reductions in tariff even if there had been no Geneva agreements and that by this legislation he is merely implementing the terms of his budget speech. It is common ground and we should all like to make as much progress as possible, with due respect to the importance of the matters with which we are dealing. But does the minister consider it imperative to proceed with the consideration of this bill before dealing with the Geneva agreements? There is bound to be debate on them; it is just possible that the government, as a result of that debate, might come to a different view with regard to some of the items which are in the bill under discussion. Would it not be wise to discuss and dispose of the Geneva agreements before dealing with this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tariff changes here are pretty minor as compared with the proposed changes in the Geneva agreements. There are some changes here which could not wait until the Geneva agreements were disposed of. We are not deprived of our freedom of action, and if it is desirable in the interests of Canada to change the tariff rates under the Geneva agreements we can deal with them. For instance, the rate on mining machinery, face-loading machines, belt trough conveyers and so on is fixed at ten per cent, and after considering tariff matters we concluded that it would be desirable to make that free.

If you reduce the rates under this bill, are you compelled later on, under the

Income War Tax Act
Geneva agreements, if they are approved, to raise them again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend was not in his place when I answered that question, which was asked by the hon. member for St. John-Albert. I repeat, we have complete freedom of action. Certain types of mining machinery which, under the agreement, carry ten per cent we are putting on the free list. If the time comes when we do not want to continue that, and the mining industry is loaded up, we can go back to the ten per cent rate.
There is no compulsion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. Our freedom is complete. The proposed changes I am making here are desirable, no matter what happens to the Geneva agreements, and for that reason I submit we should proceed with them.

speechtext: Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 330, to amend the Income War Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, I shall have quite a few words to say on this motion, as the minister no doubt expects. Neither the budget nor this bill provides relief, except in one point which I shall mention, in respect of the taxation of cooperatives or the co-operative set-up.
I point out to the house that a submission was made to the government on behalf of the co-operative congress of Canada in March of this year. I wish to quote from that submission or brief for the benefit of the house and so that I may have it on the record. It is a long brief and I will not quote extensively from it, but there are several paragraphs which in my opinion are worthy of being incorporated in the record. I quote:
This submission is made jointly on behalf of the co-operative union of Canada and le eonseil canadien de la co-operation, and at the specific and unanimous request of the Canadian cooperative congress which wras held in Saskatoon on March 9, 10 and 11, 1948.
The congress which is the annual meeting of the co-operative union of Canada, was attended by representation from all provinces. Official representatives of le eonseil canadien de la cooperation, the French-language national association of co-operatives, were in attendance and gave approval to the resolutions passed by congress.
It also should be emphasized once again that the organizations we represent are neutral as to party politics, racial divisions and religious denominations. Because of this fundamental principle, _ common to both organizations, they are, working together, an effective and increasing influence in promoting national unity in Canada.
That should never be forgotten. Two other sections, in my opinion, should be mentioned at this time. In the submission they point out that co-operatives have been a useful and stabilizing influence during these years of rising living costs, and in that connection they state:
The past year has been one of rising costs of living. The one and one-half million people whom we represent, grouped in more than 4,500 co-operatives, have been working hard in their co-operatives attempting to maintain fair prices, and in particular they have been effecting savings for consumers of low and moderate income groups. It is submitted that they have also been a check on monopolistic practices and have been of general economic benefit to the country as a whole.
Further on, following the same line, they
say:
Two dangers which are very real today are avoided or at least minimized'-on the one hand, private profit monopoly, and on the other, excessive state control.
With these sentiments I agree most heartily, and I wish to go on now to quote from the actual resolution. The resolution consists of ten paragraphs with which I shall deal in turn. Before doing so, however, I should like to put the preamble on record:
Whereas the Minister of Finance stated in the House of Commons in 1947 that if the amendment to the Income War Tax Act did not work out equitably to co-operatives, consideration would be given to amending the act;
And whereas the co-operative movement is satisfied that the present act is impractical and inequitable;
Therefore be it resolved:	That this congress
urge upon the government of the Dominion of Canada to implement the following amendments to the Income War Tax Act and to the proposed revision thereof known as Bill 454. That is to say:
And I start with the first paragraph:
(1) That the 3 per cent provision be removed.
On other occasions I have spoken of this particular provision in the co-operative field of taxation and pointed out that it was unfair and worked a hardship on the co-operatives themselves.
I want to quote again some statistics that are embodied in the brief presented by the co-
Income War Tax Act

operative union, and I am reading from page 5 of their brief:
A year ago we submitted that certain provisions of the present Income War Tax Act were serious hindrances to co-operative enterprises and we dealt at some length with the three per cent feature of the act. It will be recalled that this provides for a minimum income tax on an amount equal to three per cent of capital employed subject to certain deductions. Co-operatives regard this provision as inequitable and it has been the cause of widespread and sustained criticism. It has been suggested to us on various occasions when we asked for the repeal of the three per cent provision that it should be given a fair trial and that we should then report on our experience. We can report that the dissatisfaction has increased and the impracticability of this and other features of the present legislation has been

That bears out the statement which this brief presents when they said, as I quoted before, that they have given it a fair trial and find it has caused wide-spread and sustained criticism.
In dealing with that particular section I want to point out, as I have stated many times in this house, that the provision to tax cooperatives on three per cent of the capital employed is arbitrary and unjust. In fact it is a deliberate move to prevent any attempt on the part of people to establish non-profit businesses. I think it was the bon. member for Danfort.h (Mr. Harris) who the other day accused the minister of not having intestinal fortitude. I do not make that accusation against him. I think he has plenty of it, with a capital "G". However I think it is his judgment that is at fault. I think it is a lack of wisdom or a lack of wise advice that is causing him to take this unfair action with regard to co-operative associations.
I just want to analyse for a minute or two, if I may, the sources of capital employed in a co-operative association. It is money invested voluntarily by the members in one of three ways. It may be (a) share capital or membership fee; it may be (b) loan capital supplied by the member; or it may be (c) money borrowed from any other money-lender

to carry on the business. With respect to (a) and (b) there is no justification for any government to make a law enforcing a free people to declare a profit on money invested by themselves for the purpose of doing business with themselves. If the investors wish to declare a profit to themselves, that is their affair; and, conversely if they do not, that is also their affair. But this government has arbitrarily forced them to declare a profit. It has done so solely for the purpose, in my opinion, of pacifying its big business friends, the income taxpayers' association and their members.
I want to point this out. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) of this government and the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), who are not here today, who profess affection for the co-operatives on every occasion on wrhich they can give lip service to them, have failed to intercede on behalf of the co-operatives, even though they claim to espouse their cause. There can be nothing but condemnation for them, this government and the Liberal party if this is not changed. I want to say to my hon. friends over to my right, the Progressive Conservatives, I sincerely hope that the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) will be able and willing to persuade his party to oppose this type of

Income War Tax Act
law. I hope that some of the Liberal members for Quebec will oppose it when they realize that their French-speaking organization in Quebec has also joined with the other co-operatives in the country in the presentation of this brief.
With regard to money borrowed from other sources-that is, the money which is not provided by the members themselves-it is borrowed on the open market. The price to be paid for it in the form of interest is agreed upon at the time the transaction is made. Therefore it should have no place in the statutes of this country as providing a basis for taxation. The co-operatives pay all the other taxation levied. They pay all their property and service taxes, licence fees and everything else in the localities and provinces in which they are located; but to say deliberately they are profit-making institutions when the people who put their money into them say they are not profit-making institutions, that their profits are distributed among themselves as they save money in the operation of their business; and to pass a law saying they cannot do that in this country, is, in my opinion, a direct negation of democratic procedure and free enterprise.
The next resolution reads:
That co-operatives of the type described in section 4(p) of the Income War Tax Act (section 64 of Bill 454) irrespective of the date of their incorporation, in computing taxable income be permitted to deduct from undistributed surplus limited contingency reserves which are required to be set aside by provincial law; not exceeding 10 per cent of the net earnings in one fiscal year.
That seems to me a reasonable request. The co-operative laws in our province, at least, require certain reserves to be set up for the protection of the membership. It is purely to ensure that the equity and interests of the membership are at all times protected. They do not ask for large reserves. All they ask in this resolution is that up to ten per cent of their earnings may be set aside as non-taxable; and they agree that if the amount of the reserve they desire to set up is larger than the minister feels necessary, any other reserves may be taxed. So I think the request contained in this resolution is reasonable.
Then resolution No. 3:
That the definition of "payment" 'be extended to include the application of patronage dividends on account of loans or shares or other obligations pursuant to by-law where such amounts are authorized to be applied by the by-law.
It should not be necessary to ask for this. Many members of co-operative associations do not have large sums of money at their disposal.
They wish to join the association and partake of what they believe will be the benefits. So they make a commitment; they buy a share, or so many shares, and commit themselves to lend so much capital for the operation of the business. But they cannot pay it all in cash, so they say the balance may be deducted from any patronage dividends payable to them in future as a result of the business they do with their own association. If the by-laws permit this, we consider it only fair that the minister should allow these payments to be made, and that this amount of money should not be taxable in the hands of the co-operative. If the goods bought which created the patronage, however, were used for productive purposes, that would become income in the hands of the individual when he received it.
Resolution No. 4 states:
That in view of the impossibility of estimating taxable income until after the deduction of patronage dividends, co-operatives be not required to pay income tax on the instalment basis.
The instalment payment of taxes may have been a good provision for some. The minister knows, however, or should know-and if he does not I am going to tell him as often as opportunity presents itself, until I am convinced that he does know-that patronage dividends are not declared until the annual meeting. The fiscal year must be completed. Stocktaking must be carried out. There must be an audit of the business. The reports of the stocktaker, the manager and the auditor must come before the board of directors, who, on the basis of those reports, prepare their annual reports to the shareholders. The annual meeting may be called at any time within three months after the end of the fiscal year, depending on when these reports are ready. Of course the directors may recommend certain patronage dividends, but they cannot say those will be paid until the annual meeting has received the reports, analysed them and agreed to or altered the recommendations of the directors. So it is absolutely impossible for the manager of a co-operative association to make an instalment payment on patronage dividends in the middle of the year with any degree of accuracy. Therefore I believe this provision should be included in this bill, or in any other bill the minister may bring in, preferably right away, to get it over with.
Resolution No. 5 reads:
That the term of exemption of new co-operatives be extended from three to five years.
That is not an unreasonable request. It is something the minister should be more than willing to grant. Before the war, three years
Income War Tax Act

was a reasonable length of time. All the best people were not employed; you could find competent people, or get those who could be rapidly trained. Material for building and goods for stocking the shelves were not in short supply, as they are now. As a result, a co-operative could establish itself fairly well in a three-year period. Certainly today, however, it requires at least five years; so I believe the minister should bring in the necessary amendment to give them five years free of tax in order to get themselves established.
Then resolution No. 6:
That new co-operatives, in order to have the benefit of said section 4 (p) (section 64 of Bill 454) be permitted to have np to 10 per cent of its membership persons other than individuals.
We appreciate the concession the minister has made in this respect in the bill now before us. We are very glad of that, because many local groups such as the board of a community hospital, a school board, a municipal council, or other little organizations, may wish to avail themselves as units of the benefits of co-operative enterprises operating in their areas.
Resolution No. 7 states:
That religious and educational institutions be specifically included in the list of corporations which may be members of a tax exempt cooperative credit society.
This is extremely important. Many churches in our province, of various denominations, give a great deal of time and study to the operation of credit unions and societies. Having certain financial obligations of their own, they not only set an example by helping to form these associations but wish to patronize them as units. I do not think the minister should have difficulty in finding it in his heart and in his mind to embody this resolution in the income tax laws.
Then resolution No. 8 reads:
That associations incorporated or registered under provincial co-operative legislation, or incorporated as a co-operative under dominion authority for the purposes of providing medical and hospital services, telephone services, distribution of electric power, be exempt from income taxes.
Resolution No. 9 is very similar:
That associations organized under provincial statute for providing co-operative housing ibe exempt from income tax.
Everyone knows we need an extension of hospital services. Only a few days ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) gave an indication of what the federal government was prepared to do in connection with this and other social services, in co-operation with the provinces. Telephone service is necessary 
in this country now. The way business is done today, the way affairs are carried on, a telephone is no longer a luxury. The supply of electric power is expanding as rapidly as material, power sources and labour can be found. The demand is there. Many local associations like to do these things on a co-operative basis.
The same is true of housing. My goodness, we have had so much discussion of housing in this chamber that no one can be unaware of the great need for it. Many people believe, as they have a right to believe, whether or not others agree with them, that a co-operative housing enterprise can do certain things better than they are being done by other agencies in this country. And if we call this a free country, with the right of free association, free enterprise and everything else, there should be no hesitation on the part of the government in granting this request.
The last resolution, No. 10, states:
That the section dealing with credit unions be clarified to permit societies not incorporated or organized under provincial co-operative statute, but which are registered thereunder or subject thereto, to be members of co-operative credit societies without endangering the tax-free position of the latter.
That is a simple request. There may be an agricultural society registered in a locality, but not incorporated under any act of incorporation. There may be several small local bodies which have local community interests they are trying to promote and develop for the good of the community in which they operate. They may wish to make use of credit unions and credit societies. Yet at the present time they may not become members as units of that credit union or credit society because they endanger the tax structure of the society of which they propose to become members.
I have spoken as briefly as I could, but I do not want it to be felt that, because I have been brief, I am not sincere in what I have said. I have been as emphatic as I could be. If we do not get some relief we shall have to continue this fight both in and out of the house until we get it. Everything asked for in this resolution is justifiable. It hurts no one in Canada, although it may hurt the feelings of those people who think they have the God-given right to run this country entirely by means of profit-making enterprises. If some of us feel that we want to get together and operate our affairs without making profit for anyone, but that we wish to pay decent wages to our personnel, no man in this country should come along and say.

You are going to be a profit-making institution first, and a patronage dividend1 cooperative distribution institution afterwards. So far as we can see, what we ask for is nothing but fair, if we believe in our democratic, social and economic institutions. I should like to see the minister accept these amendments at the present time, and bring every one of them forward.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take only a few moments of the time of the house to place before the minister a certain problem arising in the Leduc area of Alberta, and in other areas where drilling for oil is taking place.
As the minister is aware, under the Income War Tax Act anyone receiving a royalty from the drilling of oil has been subject to high income tax, whereas those who sell their lands to oil companies for lump sums are not taxed because they are considered to have accumulated capital gain in the process. This definitely works against those who have sold their land on a royalty basis.
Representations have been made to me to place this matter before the minister so that relief may be granted to those farmers who may have been ill-advised in selling their land on a royalty basis. In considering this problem it may be well to keep in mind that farmers who may receive royalties for one or two years may not receive any more at the end of that time. If their present income is taxed away from them they will not be able to provide for their families in the future. I would suggest that the minister fix a certain sum for each child-perhaps $25,000, or something of that kind-at which point a tax could be applied. This would bring the procedure more in line with present-day conditions in connection with people who sell their lands to oil companies for lump sums.
I did not know under what section of the bill this matter could be discussed properly, but I was anxious that the minister give the matter serious attention. I would direct the minister's attention particularly to sections 3 and 32 of the act. I am sure if this matter is given consideration many people around Leduc and Lloydminster would be most grateful.
