Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was replying briefly to the remarks made by the hon. member for Swift Current in his representations for certain changes with regard to co-operative taxation. I had dealt with various suggestions advanced by the hon. member, and I propose now to touch on the recommendation that the term of exemption be extended from three years to five years. I wish to say that the government went exceptionally far in its original bill in permitting the extension for a period of three years, quite apart from the further extension of five years.
May I briefly illustrate what I consider the unfair position in carrying on a business in Canada at the present time. Mr. A may be doing business under what we term the free enterprise system as we have it at the present time. He buys $100,000 worth of stock and marks it up 25 per cent, which gives him a gross profit of $25,000. From that is deducted his operating expenses of $15,000, which gives him a net profit of $10,000. On the basis of our taxation today he pays into the exchequer 30 per cent, or $3,000, permitting him either to invest in his business or to set aside the balance of $7,000. That is the situation of one merchant, Mr. A.
Mr. B, who is just down the street in the same community, is operating under a cooperative scheme. He is just starting out, or the co-operatives may have come along and said, We will buy your business and put you in as manager. Under that arrangement he buys $100,000 worth of stock and marks its up 25 per cent and makes his 125,000. His operating expenses will be the same as those of the other merchant, giving him the same net profit as the other merchant. Under the present government co-operative taxation scheme he is permitted to put that whole reserve of $10,000 aside. That goes on for two, three, four or five years, and the only charge against it is the three per cent on the increased capital.
To be fair to both men, my contention is that they should enjoy exactly the same system of taxation. My whole case is built on that. Instead of giving the new co-operative store the advantage of three years' exemption, I say it should be put on the same footing as the merchant who operates his own store. Instead of that, the hon. member for Swift Current asks for a further extension from three years to five years. Naturally, on general principles, I am opposed to any such further extension.
In closing, I wish to repeat what I said before. I have no objections to co-operatives forming themselves into groups to purchase for the benefit of their members. If they can effect a saving for their members, that is fine; but I do say that they should carry on business in the same way as the ordinary merchant and not create unfair competition.
May I enlarge on the reserves? In a short time they would have sufficient funds in their reserves to put in a new attractive store front, rearrange their lighting and make a very much more attractive store than the other merchant. If that were done it would be only natural for customers, whether members of the co-operative union in that particular group, or non-members, whom they are permitted to serve, to patronize them, and they will increase their business to such an extent that finally they will drive the other man out of business, although he may be giving just as good service, but because of the increased benefits which co-operatives have they would be in a very much favoured position.
I say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that is my objection to any extension of the exemption from three to five years.

Briefly I want to support the arguments presented by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), and to reply for a moment or two to the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) who, I know, has presented sincerely his argument from his point of view. His argument and his point of view are conditioned by traditional business practice and by his failure to appreciate the social dynamic of the co-operative movement in this country which is moving toward that new social order so widely advertised by his party during the last election.
In my constituency I have one of the largest co-operative developments, based on population, of any in Canada. We have consumer cooperatives, service co-operatives and producer co-operatives. Consumer co-operatives, Mr. Speaker, are simply groups of people, a mutual association of people, who have joined together in order to purchase goods at cost. After the services are provided for, the profit that the hon. member refers to which is not a profit; but simply an overcharge, is returned to members in the form of patronage dividends. These people are shareholders. The owners and the customers are almost identical. They are not in business to make a profit. They are simply a mutual association of people organized to purchase goods at cost.
Income War Tax Act

With regard to service co-operatives, in my constituency we have a number of co-operatives that have been organized to provide transportation services, to which thousands of men belong. Fewer than ten years ago these men were paying for transportation to work in the plants of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company nearly twice as much as they pay today. They decided to join together to reduce costs. They are mutual associations of working people, joined together to provide transportation at cost, and therefore any patronage dividends which may be obtained at the end of the year is simply a return of an overcharge retained till then in order to make for the.sound operation of the business.
With respect to the producer co-operatives, exactly the same situation applies. Groups of fruit growers joined together for the better *marketing of their products, not with the idea of making a profit, but for the more efficient marketing of the things that they have to sell. In their ease what is actually termed a dividend, is the balance due on previous underpayments. That is the main point. A co-operative is not formed for profit. It is a mutual association for the advantage of those concerned, who are actually doing business with themselves.
Then there is the other aspect of the question. Not only is there an advantage to individuals in savings and service costs, such as in transportation, and more efficient marketing in producer co-operatives, but there are tremendous social services that are rendered by co-operatives in Canada. In my own constituency the co-operative movement has been of great service to the district as a whole. It has done a great deal to improve the morale of the working people in that district.
This association, this working together with a common objective, not with the idea of profit or gain from the ordinary business angle, but with the idea of co-operating for the common good, which characterizes these consumer service co-operatives and producer co-operatives is rendering a great service to the community at large. This is true not only in the economic field but in the field of education as well. All true co-operatives live up to the principles of the association and set aside a certain amount of reserves for educational purposes. I maintain, therefore, that, apart from the opposition economic argument, which I fully appreciate, as presented by the senior hon. member for Halifax, the social desirability of co-operatives justifies the government, even from the free-enterprise point of view, in removing this three per cent tax on reserves, and thereby giving the cooperatives every opportunity to function, not

as strictly business organizations but as mutual associations operating to the advantage of the community as a whole.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): I wish to ask the minister a few questions-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do that in committee. This is second reading.

I beg your pardon. I thought we were in committee. I wish to make it clear that I am opposed to income taxes at this very high rate. I think it is detrimental in many ways and unfair.
During the war, men were giving up their lives; people generally gave up their comfort and possessions, and it behooved those who were not in the fighting line to make every sacrifice to ensure victory. The war is over, and while we still labour under a heavy burden of taxation, it is not well that that burden should be continued at the present rates.
The minister has found it convenient to produce a table which gives the impression that the income tax in this country, in the lower brackets at any rate, is less burdensome than it is in the United States. The question which I wished to ask the minister was whether or not there are any states in the union which have a higher income tax than the state of New York. I have not his facilities for obtaining information, but I am informed that no state has a higher income tax than the state of New York and that many states have a much lower income tax than that state. Even so, even though the income tax of the state of New York which he has added to the federal tax to arrive at an American total were the average income tax of all the states of the union, I doubt very much whether the comparison would be complete and entirely reliable.
We have a range of taxation, a spread of taxation which is not equalled in the United States. We have taxed almost every commodity which it is possible to tax, and I doubt very much whether the United States shows an equally broad range of taxation.
The effect of taxation is far-reaching indeed. In some cases it stifles initiative. It tends to reduce the energy and interest of the individual and it also tends to practices which possibly are legal but- not commendable.
I have a pronounced feeling that the continuation of high taxation after the end of the war is but a phase of a malady which afflicts the present administration. They have administered the affairs of everybody so successfully, if one listens to their own account of their administration, that they feel it is almost their duty to continue to devote

Income War Tax Act
their paternal inclinations to the welfare of the Canadian public at large.
They cannot give back to the people the administration of their own affairs, because they do not consider that the people are quite capable of administering their own affairs.
I have noticed that the minister stated at one point in his speech, as reported at page 4056 of Hansard, that it is the policy of the government to revert to free enterprise as soon as possible. The words to which I refer are these:
The policy of the government has been to return to a free system and to moderate the inevitable increases in prices at this time by whatever fiscal and other methods are possible under such a system. Neither this government nor this parliament has either the political mandate or the constitutional power to maintain indefinitely in peace time a strait-jacket of controls over prices, production and distribution. Our whole economy has been organized to operate on a price basis by private incentives and private initiatives, not by centralized direction.
Each year the minister, whether it is the hon. gentleman who now holds that high office or his predecessor, has made statements of this kind. But, as the late A1 Smith used to say, what does the record show? The record shows that we are still in a strait-jacket. In the month of December, 1945, we enacted legislation which continued controls; and I include taxation as among the most burdensome of controls. It takes taxation to manipulate, operate and feed controls. We passed an act which made it possible to continue the controls in operation. A little later, in 1946, we passed another act called the transitional powers act. Then, in 1947, we passed another act or continuation of the act. Again in 1948, we passed another act. When I say "we", I mean parliament. The House of Commons and the Senate passed those acts. We are still a long way from a free economy and free enterprise. What is the result? The result is high taxes.
We all remember very well-at least I do- that at the first session there was a good deal of boasting done because we had emerged from the war with relatively low prices; that is, it was said they were low compared with those that applied at the end of the first great war. I do not think the government can say much today about the success of its attempt in this field. Prices are higher than they have ever been and there is little indication that they will recede. This is a result of the managed economy; and again, managed economy depends for its life and vitality upon high taxation. The government has tried about everything. The rental of houses in which we live is under control; the money which we
need to travel is under control; and the things we wish to purchase are under control; the ambit of our activity is restricted and restrained by what I will call, without any disrespect, this mania of the government to manage the affairs of the individual. Everything has been tried but the old-fashioned remedy of letting people mind their own business and affairs. If the government, in its search for some way out of the difficult general situation in which we find ourselves-and we are short of dollars; we are short of commodities; we are short of freedom-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I must call his attention to the fact that we are on the second reading of a bill entitled "An Act to amend the Income War Tax Act." I believe that he should confine his remarks to the principle of the bill which is before the house.

Thank you for your suggestion, Mr. Speaker. I was merely seeking, in the broad field which I was covering, to show how universal is the malady which attaches to the practice, a shining example of which is the burdensome income tax which is now under discussion.
I had hoped that the government would reduce the income tax for the people in the lower brackets and for the people in the higher brackets. The people in the higher brackets are not suffering because they have not enough to eat, enough with which to clothe themselves or because they are not able to house themselves ; but the general business of the country is suffering through the restrictions that are put upon the normal activities of normal people by burdensome and almost punitive taxation. I had hoped that, in this third budget which has been introduced after the war, some relief would be afforded to all those who suffer under all these taxes, and especially under the income tax act.

Taxes in the country, Mr. Speaker, are dismaying our people. In moving around among the people in the city of Ottawa-and I refer to ordinary people like streetcar conductors and other men with about the same standard of living-I find that they are completely dismayed at the situation which confronts them by reason not only of the income taxes which are being levied but also by the property taxes and the sales taxes levied on foods and other things which they must have. Therefore they feel that they are threatened with being crushed under the burden of taxation. May I tell the minister that I realize, as I believe he does, that he is getting the stage
Income War Tax Act

all set for communism when he gets the people in despair; and he has the people throughout this country in despair.
Preparing for revolt.

He is absolutely driving the people till they simply do not see how they will make ends meet at all. As has been said many times in this house, present prices are completely disheartening, and many kinds of goods are of poor quality. They do not last. Only this morning I was thinking of the matter of shoes. When I was a small boy if my parents were willing to forgo high-class attractiveness in shoes and buy what we might call stogies, they could get a pair of shoes that would stand up for a good many months rough wear on the part of a youngster. You cannot get shoes like that now. You get what apparently are stogies, and in about a month you find your child has gone through a lot of paper and his feet are on the ground. That is a serious matter which must be kept in mind.
Incomes generally are too low. That has been stated a good many times; but in this chamber we must keep constantly before us, and the minister in particular must keep before him, what must be the point of view of the average mind, the average industrial worker, or white-collar w'orker, as he contemplates the economic situation. We are railing against communism, as though we had an idea that merely railing against a thing would do away with it. Meanwhile we are adopting exactly the policies which must have influenced the people of Czechoslovakia, for example, when they permitted the iron curtain to descend upon them. Those people found themselves confronted with a situation which confounded them, and they said, "Nothing could be any worse than this. Let us give communism a try".
They tried the socialists first, did they not?

I suppose they did. Certainly they tried something. With the lack of information prevailing throughout the dominion today, people are just as likely to try communism as anything else, because, after all, they just do not know enough about economics to be able to tell one ism from another.
In addition, there is a great deal of worry about the coming of a depression. I find that the ordinary person with a little money invested or a little property is almost paralysed with anxiety. He asks, "Why is it we must have these depressions? What is the matter with the people in charge? They wring their hands and shrug their silly shoulders and act

as though depressions were a sort of act of God and they had nothing in the world to do with them. Well, what is the good of a government if it cannot control depressions? What is a government for if it is not to control depressions, and what is it doing to try to control depressions?" These are the questions that are in the minds of ordinary men.
All these things, Mr. Speaker, have an important bearing upon the measure now before us, which proposes to levy such a heavy rate of income tax on those in the low-income brackets. May I earnestly submit to the minister that there simply must be a change. We just cannot go on as we have been going on. Other conditions are changing. There must be a change in our way of doing things. If the minister can find out what that change should be and propose it, we will listen to his proposal. If he cannot find a suitable change, then I submit that he should be listening to us. And if he does not have a change there will be either communism or chaos; the result will be the same in either case.
In my judgment a change in our financial system will remove the bottleneck which is obstructing a solution of our problem. I have served on committees at various times during the last few years. I am deeply impressed with the feeling of impotence and utter helplessness that seems to prevail among the members of committees. It is as though they were trying to make headway against a hurricane or a giant flood or something of that sort.
Our present financial system provides abundantly for the creation of money to lend for production. Our financial system refuses to create money to spend for distribution. I point out to the minister that in my judgment this is the fundamental fallacy in our financial system today.
Let me repeat that, not only for the benefit of the minister but also for the benefit of the men who are advising the minister. I sometimes get the impression that the minister has so many problems confronting him that he is unable to give these matters the thought and study he would like to give them, and that as a result he has to depend upon the men who are advising him. Then we must talk to the men advising the minister, and they are the ones to whom I am talking now; not only to the minister but, through him, to the men behind him all the way down from the deputy minister to those members of the finance department who are in the galleries here tonight. I am warning them that if they do not make this country's financial system work, they will be to blame. They just cannot tinker around with the sort of financial system we have had during the last century and a half. We are in

Income War Tax Act
a world of change. It is their business to find out the kind of change that is necessary in our financial system to meet changed conditions, and to make recommendations to the minister in accordance with their findings.
May I point out again that our financial system readily creates money to create debt, but that it refuses to create money to retire debt. The result is that debt is accumulating throughout the country in every direction; not only nationally, provincially and municipally, but on the part of corporations and other organizations. This kind of thing obviously must not be permitted to go on. Surely our generation has not been brought into being to be crushed by debtl Surely the mere fact that we have had to go through a number of wars ought not to condemn us forever to debt or to taxation that will destroy us in order to pay off that debt. We should be able to pay off debt with goods; and if this country can produce enough goods it should be able to pay off its debts. I give that to the members of the finance department who are advising the minister. If you have not a system under which the production of goods and services in Canada will pay off Canada's debt, then you have a financial system that needs serious revamping.
The hon. gentleman should address the Chair.

Very good; I am
addressing Mr. Speaker. In my judgment our financial system must be geared to create money adequately to distribute goods and services, as well as to produce them. It must be geared to produce money adequately, gradually to liquidate our debt in a sound way, not by taxing the people into complete despair but by changing the goods-producing power of the people into money. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), I move this amendment:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that this house do resolve that the federal government should consider the advisability of setting up a royal commission on banking and currency to ascertain to what extent it might be practicable to finance the affairs of Canada by means other than taxation or debt.
I have no desire to detain the house unduly, but I wish to lay down simply and straightforwardly to the house and the minister nine reasons why I believe it is appropriate that we should propose this amendment, that the house should vote for it and that the government should act upon it.
In the first place, the soundness of the principle of creating money debt-free is recognized by the best informed economic thinkers in the world today.
May I, as one illustration, cite the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, chairman of the Midland Bank in Britain, in a speech he delivered on January 30, 1936, to be found in an article in the London Times of that date, at oage 23. In that article he states:
Additional currency however can now be furnished by the authorities, if they choose to exercise their powers, without reference to the Central Bank's holding of gold. Thus the 19th century which brought into general use a means of payment hitherto scarcely known outside London, brought also the machinery whereby it could be subjected to intelligent control.
That statement, coming from a responsible man like Reginald McKenna, constitutes a challenge to every man who has anything to do with the financial affairs of the Dominion of Canada or any other state in the world, and it constitutes a challenge to members of this House of Commons.
May I submit, following that quotation, that our age must adopt this new.means of payment, or perish. It must adopt also the machinery for controlling that new means of payment.
There are other outstanding men whose opinions must be respected. I have in mind, for instance Doctor William A. Shaw. We do not hear a great deal in Canada about Dr. Shaw, and since he made the remarks I am going to quote, perhaps it is easy to understand why.
One thing which I find quite astonishing is that the governments of Canada and the United States, and of various other members of the commonwealth, seem deliberately to ignore the great vital modern truths concerning money. Let us see who Doctor Shaw is. He is editor of "The Calendar of Treasury' Records" at His Majesty's public records office; author of the "History of Currency"; author of "English Monetary Writers"; author of "Currency, Credit and The Exchanges during the Great War", published in 1926; "The Coming Reaction: by Legislator"; "Theory and Principles of Central Banking", published in 1930.
I would submit that if a man was able to write as many books as that without falling from grace entirely, and still have a reputation, it might be worthwhile to give some attention to what he has said.

State money has been used successfully, as I argued on May 24, and do not propose to re-argue at this time. The Guernsey island undoubtedly used state money, with success, as I developed on May 24, and as reported at page 4337 of Hansard. Canada, in world war I used the state money principle successfully. Around 1917 she printed 126 million and spent it without increasing the debt or taxation, or the interest load of her people.
How is it we have done nothing of that kind during the recent war? The principle worked well at the time of the first world war. Those who wish to look into the matter and get authority on it will be able to find it in the proceedings of the royal commission of 1933 on banking and currency for Canada. They will find the transaction reported particularly at page 22, paragraph 47. They will find some very interesting material concerning money in that document immediately preceding paragraph 47.
The Bradbury's in England were a form of state money. Doctor William A. Shaw has directed his attention to a discussion of the Bradbury's in several of his books, particularly in "The Theory and Principles of Central Banking", published in 1930, and "Currency, Credit and the Exchanges", published in 1926. Here are some of the things Doctor William A. Shaw says about the Bradbury's; but before quoting that, may I say the Bradbury was nothing but a treasury note. It was printed by His Majesty's treasury, just as the Minister of Finance of Canada might print a $5 bill. The Bradbury's went into circulation in Great Britain and replaced the specie money there, thus enabling Britain to finance a terrific effort to win a war.
Why should people disregard the discovery made in those Bradbury's? This, I repeat, is what Doctor Shaw says at page 72 of the "Theory and Principles of Central Banking":
By some process of evolution as yet unexplained Great Britain during the years 1945 and 1916, discovered the true principles of state issue of paper money, and benefited! unspeakably by it all through the great war. But so little did she understand what she had done that after 13 years of the practice of an automatic self-regulating issue of full price state paper money she surrendered the right once more to a monopoly bank in 1928. A fresh conception of finance and a different type of currency doctrine must emerge before the evil of this retrograde step can be removed.
And at page 75 he says:
Similarly -with regard to the treasury note issue, whilst it was in existence. There was no reason why the individual joint-stock banks

should not have gone directly to the inland revenue office for the purchase of supplies of such notes as they required, or for the surrendering of such notes as they no longer required. It would have been quite easy for the separate banks to keep each a separate account at the inland revenue offices for the purpose, and if this had been done the automatic nature of the treasury note issue would have been much more widely understood. It was only as a matter of convenience and economy of working that the treasury decided that the inland revenue should have only one account, namely with the Bank of England, and that the Bank of England should act as the wholesale house for the sale of currency to the retail banks, and for the repurchase of currency from them of such currency as they wished to surrender. So long as the treasury note was in existence, the Bank of England was not an issuer of that currency, any more than it was an issuer of gold coins when our currency consisted of gold. It was only a distributor of the one as of the other. But when the treasury note -was suppressed by the amalgamation operation of 1928 the Bank of England became once more the issuer as well as the distributor of the paper money of the nation, and the two quite separate functions of issuing and distributing currency became once again confused.
I realize that hon. members will find it somewhat difficult to follow those passages, but they have a profound meaning right now for us in this parliament and for our government. May I go on?
We create money to lend for the production of goods and services. How freely we create that- money may be learned by reference to a book in our own library called "The Canadian Banking System" by James Holladay. I refer hon. members to chapter 10, page 140. I do not quote that, because hon. members may turn to the book themselves.
What we are told there is that the Canadian banking system can take one dollar of gold and on that one dollar of gold create four $1 bills. The chartered banks can take the four $1 bills and create $20 of credit expansion for each $1 bill. This means that on the basis of $1 in gold we can create $84 of currency and credit in the Dominion of Canada. This house passed that law giving that power to the banks and showing that we have no concern at all, no fear at all of the danger of creating too much money so long as the money is created to lend for production.
Why should we be in such mortal terror- we and the members of the finance department *

of creating some money to spend for consumption, for distributing goods? Why should we consider it completely sound to create money to lend; yet consider it completely unsound to create money with which to distribute? We must create money to spend for distributing goods.

I go on with the second main reason why this amendment which I have moved is worthy of the most careful consideration of members of the house. The second main reason is that the principle which determines the amount of money that can be safely issued and employed is now pretty accurately understood. That principle is: the amount of money that can be safely issued is the amount necessary to effect the exchanges which require to be effected in the state. May I quote eminent authorities to support that statement? This is a new principle, having been discovered within the last twenty years. It is laid down definitely in William A. Shaw's work, "Currency, Credit and the Exchanges," published in i926, which I quote from page 66 as follows:
The episode of the British treasury note experiment transcends in importance any other event in the economic experience of the modern world.
I pause there while the solemnity of those words sinks in:
On the practical side it has emancipated us from the grip of an imperfect gold currency system and of a costly and cruel hank rate system. In comparison with such an achievement the erection of the federal reserve system in the United States is halting and imperfect. But the treasury note episode has not merely this practical value. It has an equally significant import in the domain of theory. By its means we have evolved the true theory of money, and in the light of this theory our currency and hanking legislation need no longer be the process of blindfold groping and experimenting which it has been in the past.
This theory of money rests upon one basic principle, viz., that goods purchase goods. In this axiom the word "goods" is used for brevity's sake as comprehending all economic goods or services which, as possessing economic value, possess thereby exchange value.
These words will repay going over about three times a day for a month or two until their importance sinks right into the thinking of the people of Canada, particularly those in authority in these troubled times.
Again on page 71 of that book he uses the following words:
By such a chain of reasoning I think it will be clear that a community's purchasing power

The third reason supporting my amendment is: Gold backing has been proved utterly unnecessary in our day. That is shown in the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna's statement which I read a moment ago. It is shown in the statement [DOT]which I have read from Doctor William A. Shaw concerning the Bradbury experiment. It is established by Canada's world war II experience. May I pause a minute? The minister can tell me whether I am wrong and the members of his department can tell me. Was not every dollar of gold in Canada taken from behind the Canadian financial structure during the war and placed behind the foreign exchange equalization fund? In other words, did not the Dominion of Canada run its whole financial structure all through the perilous time of the war without a single dollar of gold behind its financial structure as far as the domestic economy was concerned? And if they did it in the war, will they tell me why they cannot do it in peace? These questions have to be answered. They must be asked by responsible men and they must be answered by responsible men. There is only one answer, and that is in favour of the proposals of social credit, state money.
Now, Canada's Bank Act, according to a quotation to which I referred from "The Canadian Banking System" by James Holladay, shows the unimportance of gold. When a nation can take one dollar of gold and expand S84 of currency and credit for use in the nation, gold has become an extremely insignificant matter as far as domestic affairs are concerned in that nation. Then again, the suspension of the gold redemption clause by order in council on April 10, 1933, which made it illegal to have gold in the possession of the ordinary individual,

proved that there was no gold backing necessary for Canadian money; that its value did not depend on gold backing. We will find an account of that suspension in the Report of the Royal Commission on Banking and Currency in Canada, 1933, at page 22.
Again, it has been and will be argued that the introduction of state money will cause inflation. I do not propose to go into details concerning that matter, because I went into details in my speech on May 24; but let me point out to the minister, as the fourth reason supporting my proposal, that today the nature and the cause and the means of the prevention of inflation are now well understood. This last war finished giving us the information on that matter, and showed beyond a doubt that inflation does not depend on money so much as it does on goods. What I said concerning that matter will be found in the 1948 Hansard at pages 4332 and 4333.
The fifth reason is that successful price control is an established fact. This was demonstrated clearly during world war II in Britain, in the United States and in Canada. It has been said several times that, whereas price control was possible during war, it is impossible during peace, but it has never been proved. Will anyone pretend to me that if the United States, Canada and Great Britain together had decided to use the measures of control of prices which they used during the war, they could not have succeeded in peacetime, especially if they had liberated and stimulated the productive capacities in these nations? I will grant that the necessities of sending very great quantities of food and other goods to western Europe have had a considerable effect, but we could have overcome the ill effects of that sacrifice of goods had we only had wisdom enough to stimulate the productive capacities of this nation, of the United States and of other nations, instead of discouraging our farmers until they disposed of their milk cows, their swine, their beef cattle and their sheep. Whose fault was it that they disposed of all these animals? It was the fault of the governments of Canada and the United States. Surely measures could have been taken to avoid that loss of production which we have had. I say that successful price control is an established fact.
A sixth reason in supporting my proposal is:	Devices are now understood for withdrawing surplus money, redundant credit, as Social Crediters call it, from circulation when it is no longer needed in the economy. The fundamental problem which confronts the world at the present time, as every hon. member from the Minister of Finance outward knows, is a shortage of United States dollars. It is thought that we shall be able to solve the difficulty of the shortage of United States dollars by entering into some such agreement as the Geneva trade treaty. Let us not delude ourselves.
There was a shortage of United States dollars during the twenties and that shortage hadi to be made up by United States foreign' lending. Billions a year were lent by the United States to the nations of Europe to enable them to buy United States goods until the people of the United States discovered that it was not a sound method. I want to repeat what I have said on other occasions by way of emphasizing another evil which is rarely considered as a result of heavy taxation. I refer to the softening of the moral fibre of the people as the growing power of taxation in the hands of a state transforms a social government, as it was in the beginning years ago, into an anti-social state. Those things should be thought over carefully.
In my opinion here are the steps by which that transformation takes place. In the first place, as more and more of the individual's production is taken by the state in the form of taxes, the less he has for his own enjoyment and the greater effort he must make to maintain himself or to better his circumstances. The government for many years have operated on a steadily-increasing tax scale. This has resulted mainly from the fact that they have persisted in following what my colleague the hon. member for Lethbridge so well described to the house tonight as an outworn and thoroughly discredited policy of finance. As long as we persist in following such a policy, then taxation taken as a percentage of the gross national income will continue to go up.
I can remember the day in my own life when taxes in Canada represented less than seven per cent of the total national income. Today they represent somewhere between twenty-five and thirty per cent of it. The tendency is always upward. If the amount of taxes that we were taking from the people continued to rise, and at the same time our gross national production continued to rise in as great proportion or greater, I would not be so much worried about the weight of the burden of taxation. But when the proportion of national production that is taken by taxation by our government continues to increase, then I become concerned.

The second step is this. As ever-increasing proportions of the production of a person's own efforts are taken from him in taxes, the more the dignity of the individual disintegrates under the hammering of want and the fear of want. Anybody knows that is only sound reasoning, because so many of our people are forced through heavy taxation to live on the borderline of poverty or below it, not able to accumulate any reserve to meet the crises in their lives. On the other hand, the power of the state in the process, grows greater in proportion to the wealth it absorbs through the power of taxation. As it grows in power, history has shown that it has become less concerned about the individual welfare of the human resources that it governs.
In the third place, as economic power is transferred by taxation from the individual to the state, the individual often is pressed by circumstances such as illness in the family, crop failure or some other tragic circumstance, into bargaining for some of what was properly his by right of production. In the bargaining process, when he goes to the government for help he is often forced to surrender what has been considered for many years his inalienable rights, and he has to bargain with these for a hand-out from the government, because his independence is gone. The hand-out might be in the form of relief-I have seen it happen- it might be in the form of unemployment insurance; it might be a place on the public payroll or a subsidy of one kind or another. Whatever it might be, Mr. Speaker, the uneven bargain demonstrates that the non-productive state has gained economic strength and great political power through the taxing authority, while the productive individuals in the state have become merely supplicants with caps in hand, and with no spirit left. All too often that is the net result. Everywhere moral disintegration has inevitably followed upon the heels of continued high taxation. I think we saw the ultimate of this disintegration of the individual in Germany, in Russia, in Italy, in Japan, where the power of taxing made a shambles of all the property rights of the people. For further evidence we might go back in history and take a look at what happened just before the fall of the mighty Roman empire sixteen hundred years ago.
The power to tax is the power to destroy human dignity. Unless that power is used wisely and with restraint, it will destroy the moral fibre of the people. We have been witnessing that very process in this country for some time now. Never before in our history has the government of Canada been so nearly

an all-powerful state. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this represents the government; an allpowerful state. Never before has such a large portion of the wealth produced by individual Canadians been confiscated by the state. What seems to me ominous about the whole matter is that there is a growing public acceptance of the doctrine that has been preached into our people, that high state taxation is an instrument for social good. I suppose we have the Marxists and socialists, or at any rate those who call themselves such, to thank for that.

I do not want to go on year after year advocating and propagating a philosophy or policy that is not right. If we are attempting to propagate a fallacy, let us know about it. We can only know about it if some of the wise men of this country come out and attempt to show us that we are wrong. I am prepared to debate this whole policy. Is it reasonable to suppose, Mr. Speaker, that the same system which gave us all those things in the thirties can possibly give us prosperity, peace, business stability and widespread happiness now that

That has been because of the fundamental and crippling fault in the policy and system itself.
The financial structure we have today has failed for many years to distribute to the people the goods they can produce. My colleague, the hon. member for Lethbridge, mentioned Chester Bowles, a man of some authority, held in high regard to certain circles, and I should like to emphasize one thing Chester Bowles said. He spoke of the income of the lowest third of the people in the United States; and I quote him only because there is no similar work in Canada. We need one, and in times past I have advocated that we have something of the kind of survey done by Mr. Bowles, but it has not been done. According to Chester Bowles, the income of the lowest third of the people in the United States in 1940, which in the aggregate was nine per cent of the total, was an average of $527. That was in 1940, a war year. Can anyone say that the financial policy being followed by the government of the United States, which is essentially tfie policy followed by the government of Canada, was doing a good job of distribution in getting to the lowest third of the people in that country an average of only $527 a year? That would not give them protective foods such as citrus fruits, milk, eggs, butter and meat. Even the middle third of the people, according to the charts on page 69 of this book, had an average income of only $1,311. How could they possibly live and give their children anything like a decent opportunity for education, cultural growth and moral standing with an income of that kind? The average income in the top third was $3,722. That is getting more like it.
I mention these matters merely because here we have evidence that the financial policies being followed both in Canada and in the
United States have failed. Therefore it seems most pressing that we effect a change. When I say it is time to effect a change I should like for a moment to examine two or three statements made in this remarkable little document which was mentioned by the hon. member for Lethbridge, and which, as a matter of fact, I read on his recommendation in the first place. It is called "The United States in the World Economy," and is written by eminent authorities in the department of commerce of the United States. It is issued under the name of Jesse H. Jones, secretary of commerce and O. P. Hopkins, of the bureau of foreign and domestic commerce; and was written by Hal B. Lary, with a foreword by Wayne Taylor, under-secretary of commerce.
As I read this book all the way through.
I found time after time these men emphasizing one important point, and I wish to refer to just one or two places where this particular point is emphasized. At page VI of the introduction to the book, these men have this to say:
The functioning of the American economy as a whole presents some of the most baffling problems. On the solution of these problems, through maintenance of a high and reasonably stable level of economic activity in the United States, the interests of this country and of other countries are most clearly and indisputably united.
Then again at page 200 in a final word, they have this to say:
Whatever may be the other requirements, stability in international economic relations generally and in foreign exchange rates in particular cannot be assured1 solely or chiefly through technical financial arrangements-
Such as Bretton Woods, and the like.

but must be firmly based on a vigorously and regularly functioning domestic economy.
That is about the fifteenth time I have noticed the same emphatic statement throughout this work. What does it mean? It means simply this; it is a warning by these men who issued the work in 1944 that there could be no hope whatever for a world peace, and for that ideal condition of world trade, unless and until the United States itself began to bring order into its own internal economy and make it work smoothly. The same can be said of Canada also.
And, Mr. Speaker, other experts such as Beardsley Ruml. Professor C. E. Ayres and others have pointed out that the only way in which the internal American economy can be made to work smoothly is to see to it that the financial system is changed, that the financial policy is altered so that the
Income War Tax Act

full production of the United States can be distributed in their own land to all of the people.
I was interested in an editorial which appeared not long ago-as a matter of fact, on May 5-in the Montreal Star, criticizing my colleague the hon. member for Lethbridge. The editorial is headed "Discredited Critic". I wish to refer to only one thing the Montreal Star did say. It said:
We shouldn't like our American friends to think that when John Blackmore gets up in the House of Commons and criticizes the United States he speaks for any substantial body of Canadian opinion. He doesn't. Mr. Blackmore is one of the small Social Credit group whose ideas revolve around a thoroughly discredited theory of funny money.
That represents the expression of a mischievous editorial writer who likes to stick his nose into other people's business and make categorical statements with little possibility of ever having to be called to account. He is one of the type of petrified pip-squeaks-if that is a parliamentary expression-who know nothing whatever about economics, but who are so inflated with the idea that they are qualified to mould public opinion on any subject whatever, that they rush in at every opportunity to make the world think they know something.
This fellow was no exception. I do not know why this editorial writer did light into my hon. friend the member for Lethbridge, but I am sure it was not because anything the hon. member for Lethbridge had said was disproved; because all the hon. member for Lethbridge said on this particular occasion he quoted from authorities in the United States-and from this book, "The United States in the World Economy."
But the Montreal Star comes along and says that the hon. member is a thoroughly discredited critic, and that it does not want people in the United States to think that what the hon. member has said represents a large body of Canadian thought.
I just wish to say this to the editorial writer of the Montreal Star, that I should like to have him produce the evidence that Social Credit is thoroughly discredited. I will be prepared to have him conduct in his own paper a thorough discussion of social credit principles.
I will guarantee, Mr. Speaker, that he will demonstrate he has never read them and does not know anything about them. And I shall answer him here from the floor of the House of Commons, or in his own paper.
I am reminded of one of the proverbs that says this:	"Who condemns ignorance is
twice accursed." That often is the condition of mind exhibited by these so-called author-

ities who sit in armchairs in newspaper offices and attempt to mould public opinion.
Whoever did discredit the social credit philosophy? I would like to find him. I would like him to trot out his stuff. And if he has not discredited it, then I would like him to keep quiet. But for my own peace of mind I would like to see one real, honest effort made; one that gets down to details and comes to grips with the true facts; one which takes consideration of scientific argument, logic and reason, in an effort to show to the world that social credit principles are discredited. But until that does happen no editorial writer has a right to claim that this philosophy which we advocate is in any way discredited. I say to this editorial writer that, by making sweeping categorical statements in ignorance, he is thoroughly discredited.
In closing, let me say to the minister that I have a full appreciation of what he is up against. As long as he is operating under the present financial policy he cannot do very much more than he is doing. I know that. I know, too, that he is a bright boy; and I know, further, that if he would take just a little while and examine the amazing array of evidence we have already placed upon the record here, I am satisfied he would soon come to. a conclusion. Then, if he would step into the House of Commons and give us his honest decision, his honest opinion as a result of having examined those things and of having weighed them carefully, I would be a very happy man.
If I am found wrong, I will be the first to admit to the Minister of Finance that I was wrong. But I must be shown; and until I am shown, I shall continue to advocate the policy in which I believe. I favour the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Lethbridge, because I feel sure a careful, honest investigation by a royal commission will reveal that there is a better way of financing our government than by continued debt and high taxation.

Mr. Speaker, I addressed the house at some length on the resolution stage of the bill; therefore I have only one or two observations I wish to make at this time.
In the first place, I wish to recall to the mind of the minister that when previously I spoke on the resolution I suggested to him that there were certain reductions and reliefs which he might give. I pointed out that I did believe that budgeting for a certain amount of surplus was sound budgeting, because I believe in the repayment of debt. I suggested, however, that the amount which he contemplated was an unnecessarily large amount; I pointed out that

Income War Tax Act
in the year just past his actuality had exceeded his estimate by about $460 million; and while I did not suggest there would be any such overrun this time, I did suggest that I thought it was extremely likely that he had budgeted very conservative, and, further, that the surplus of nearly $500 million which the minister estimated for the forthcoming year was unnecessarily high.
I do not propose to traverse that ground again, but I merely wish to point out one thing. The minister indicated that there were two reasons for this surplus: one the repayment of debt and the other perhaps exceptional defence measures. I do not accept the second one as a proper reason, but I do accept the first, subject, as I said, to the proper amount.
But I wish to make one point. We are now budgeting for a surplus of some $500 million. I think I am correct in saying that the hands of the minister and of the government are not tied in any way, shape or form as to what they shall do with it. 1 think that was the reason why, when the budget speech was completed, there was apparent unanimity in this house that it indicated clearly one thing, namely, that there would be no election before there was another session of parliament.
We all know why that was. Everyone felt that this was a means of keeping a bonanza, so to speak, available for the electors and to be disclosed to them before the next election. I do not think it can be said that our electors will suppose that this is an act of benevolence on the part of the government, nor will they believe that this is the government's money. Of course they will not believe anything of the kind; nevertheless there is an advantage psychologically in a government being in a position to suggest or to bring forward large taxation reductions and other popular measures just before an election.
Therefore I suggest that it is improper that this large surplus should be left lying about loose, so to speak, when there is no tie-in in any way as to how it is to be used. If the minister refuses to accept my proposals that there should be substantial reductions in taxation at the present time, first, through an increase of the exemptions in the lower income brackets and, second, by way of tax assistance to smaller companies, then there should be some definite and binding indication as to where this money will be spent, so that the government shall not have a fund of $500 million which can be used for what we shall call election purposes.

Mr. Speaker, the Income War Tax Act has been amended nineteen times since 1927, and if this bill passes it will be the twentieth amendment of the act. That makes for cumbersome legislation, and a revision is badly needed. Three years ago the then Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) said in his budget speech that a revision of the act was overdue. Last year we were presented with Bill No. 454, to amend the Income War Tax Act.
When that bill was up for first reading, I think it was July 12, 1947, the minister said that it was not intended to proceed with the bill at that session, that it was being introduced for study and suggestions. He said that the main part of the act was cluttered up-I think those were his words-with provisions dealing with exceptional cases which had been gathered together.
He went on to say that, under the law, the minister had discretion in forty-three cases, but in the bill presented last year there were to be only two cases where the minister would have discretion. An income tax appeal board was to be set up to deal with matters in dispute, and that board would be a court of record. He intimated that the bill would come before us this year and said that it would be dated back to January 1, 1948.
For some reason or another that bill has not come before us. I notice in the bill now before us, as well as in Bill No. 454 presented to us last year, there is no mention of increased penalties to be imposed upon those people who are not able to pay their taxes on time, nor is there any provision about people who have reached the age of sixty-five years. I think we should have some explanation from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That bill will be introduced tomorrow. The resolution has been on the order paper for two or three days.
That is why I rose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I announced in my budget speech that a tremendous amount of work has been done on the bill. We have had representations from all the associations. The bill is ready and, as a matter of fact, I was hoping to introduce it tomorrow at the latest.
With the unanimous consent of the house I would be glad to withdraw my amendment in order to save the time that would be needed to take a vote.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate

Agreed.

On section 1-Co-operatives.

Can the minister state if the income tax of the state of New York, which he added to the federal tax in order to compare the United States income tax with the Canadian income tax, is the highest of all state taxes? If not, what states have higher income taxes than the state of New York, and what states have lower income taxes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not have the information with me, but I will bring it down when the other bill is brought in. The official who was in charge of that is not with me this evening. My understanding is that it is a fair average of the state income taxes in the United States. That is my information. I am relying on that.

I thought the matter was of such grave importance, and the assertion was made with such care and precision, that it would be well to find out how many states in the union have a higher income tax than New York, and how many states have a lower income tax than New York.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be very glad to get that information. I am introducing, I hope tomorrow, the Income Tax Act which we were discussing a moment ago with the hon. member for St. John-Albert, and I shall have that information available and perhaps give it then rather than hold up the committee this evening. I shall have to get the information and give it to the committee when we have the big bill before us, if that meets with my hon. friend's wishes.

I do not want to delay the bill, but I am going to suggest to the minister that he pick out some clauses which will stand and on which I can get the information. If that is agreeable, we can go on with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had rather hoped that we would be able to conclude consideration of these clauses this evening. If we cannot, of course we cannot; but I shall certainly get the information for my hon. friend and put it on Hansard, I hope within the next day or two, which I take it is what he wants. He is seeking information. He has no other purpose in his questioning.

I do not say that I am actually seeking for information alone. I am

under the impression that we have an income tax that is higher than the income tax in the United States. I wish to investigate that question rather closely, because I am one of those who feel that the country at large is suffering from an over-burden of taxation, and if it develops that our income taxation is higher than the income taxation in the United States it would be an added reason for a reduction.
I would call to the attention of the minister that a great point was made of the fact that our taxation was lower than the taxation in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only in certain brackets.

I concede that. I do not want to take in more territory than is necessary, but it was a great source of astonishment to me, and when I am astonished I like to find out whether my feeling is based on fact or whether it is just an impression that I had built up out of inadequate information. It would be a matter of great interest to the public at large to know whether income taxation in this country is lower than it is in the United States.
I am going to make this suggestion to the minister. I suggest that he let the section stand; that he do his utmost to get the information tonight, and if we get to the end of the bill and the information is not here I might wait until tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps we might continue to deal with this bill section by section, and when we get toward the end of it we shall see how we are getting along. I have given my assurance to my hon. friend and to the committee that I will get the information just as promptly as I can. I think I should be able to have it by tomorrow. I will give it to the house; if not on this bill, on the main income tax bill for which I have a resolution on the order paper. I will give it just as fully as I can get it.
I wish to make it quite clear that the information will come down in such form as can be readily used in debate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The main income tax bill will have to go through the regular stages, resolution, first reading, second reading and so on. I hope it may go to the banking and commerce committee, and then come back here for consideration in committee. The information which I shall give my hon. friend will be available for debate in the house.
