Income War Tax Act
On section 2-Exemption for taxpayer of age sixty-five.

I want to raise a point which will be very familiar to everyone in the committee. Here again we run into our old friend the question of regulation by order in council which appears in subsection 2. I wish the minister would tell us something about the regulations and the way in which this has been managed up to now. Is there a well recognized procedure, or is the thing just dealt with more or less by guess and by God when each point arises?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The language here has always been:
Such amount as the governor in council may, by regulation, allow . . .
It used to be by discretion. The amendment proposed here is to cover the case of taxes on income imposed by municipalities.
I appreciate that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend appreciates the reason why this amendment is being made. Our agreement is that we will extend it not only to taxes imposed by provinces but also to such taxes imposed by municipalities. As I understand it, the regulations have recently been published. Work has been proceeding on them for some time, and it is part of the practice which is being followed in the new Income Tax Act, of doing certain things which require some flexibility by regulation rather than by ministerial discretion. The regulations are made and published in the Canada GazeMe. They are available to the general public and, of course, being regulations they may be amended from time to time. Broadly speaking, that is the reason for the use of regulations as distinct from ministerial discretion. When we come to the main Income Tax Act my hon. friend will see the number of cases where we provide that certain things may be done by regulation. In almost all these cases some relief is being given to the taxpayer.
I may say that one of the suggestions we have had from the accountants' association and others is that we may have to return to this much maligned system of discretion. We are trying out now the rather more formal method of regulation passed by order in council and published; but I have quite a lot of reservations myself, that in the effective administration of the Income Tax Act we may at some time have to return to some
of these discretions. However I want that to be proved by the process of trial and error, and to show that all discretions are not as bad as they have been painted. That is the reasoning here.

I want to say to the minister that, while I intend to keep my powder dry, I have not believed that all discretions were irretrievably and hopelessly bad. Somebody somewhere sometime has to make a decision, and with all deference to other systems and to other officials in other countries, such limited experience as I have had in at least two other countries has made me not too prone to criticize my own. For my own satisfaction I should, like the minister to tell me just what the difference is between leaving the discretion with the minister, which meant the commissioner, or deputy minister, or the executive head, and the governor in council, because, after all, the governor in council, the cabinet, will not go into these questions. They are going to deal with them very much as a matter of course, and it seems to me that we are getting back to the discretion of the departmental head. I am not terribly disturbed by that, but I am asking the minister if there is any difference between Tweedledum and Tweedledee. That is, between the decision of the governor in council and of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The difference is this, that the ministerial discretion was exercised as discretion in individual cases, and it might, perhaps it did, vary from case to case. Where it is provided, as in this section, that a regulation is to be adopted by the governor in council, there must be formal government action, an order in council passed approving the regulation, and the regulation is published and is available to everyone. That is the difference and I think it is a very real one. In some cases it may prove to be cumbersome. In some cases there might be ministerial discretion which could be exercised as pure discretion and vary from case to case. These have been pretty well eliminated from the new act. That is what I find some difficulty in.
Suppose the governor in council passed a regulation-I will not attempt to define the type of case-wherein the minister should have complete discretion. Where would we land then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know whether the power to delegate would exist there. It would be a delegation to someone else of powers specifically conferred by the statute on the governor in council, and offhand I would ques-
Income War Tax Act

tion whether such delegation could be exercised. I think it would have to be spelled out in the regulation. The particular one here relates to taxes which the provinces may continue to levy, although they entered into an agreement with the dominion.
Can the minister tell me what provinces now impose income tax on logging and mining companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ontario and Quebec. I am informed that they have such taxes. British Columbia has a tax, and while I do not know what it is, I am told that it used to be an alternative to income tax and is a tax on gross output. My hon. friend is probably familiar with that.
It must be a royalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not personally familiar with the tax. I am relying on information given me.
Do Ontario and Quebec impose a special tax on mining and logging companies apart from royalties?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mining only. In the case of logging companies, I suppose the taxes are in the nature of stumpage dues and are probably not income tax. Those taxes are in lieu of royalties.
They must be royalties. I do not think they are income taxes in the seven provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably not. In the case of mining companies in three provinces they are.
But that is a royalty per ton, I should think.
I want to come back to the question of regulations. As I understand it, the minister says regulations are in existence and have been published in the Canada Gazette.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told they were completed within the last month or so on this particular section.
Am I correct in thinking that those regulations, as they have been described by the minister, really become by incorporation a part of the statute law for the moment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a fair statement, yes.
Then should we not know what they are? Are we not in effect approving this when we pass this section? Is it not just as if it were virtually a part of this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This section has been in existence for some time, and in passing a provision of this kind parliament authorizes the governor in council to adopt regulations. The only amendment here is to extend the purview of the section to cover municipal cases. We are not putting in any new principle. The regulations have to be made public and parliament can get them in the Canada Gazette, or individual members can read them. It is not, however, customary to debate regulations in parliament. I shall be glad to provide them. All regulations of this kind are made public and this is not a new departure in this act. It is a fairly common practice, and has been for years, for parliament to authorize the governor in council to make regulations on certain specified subjects.

Like the hon. member for Stanstead, I will not take a fanatical position with regard to the regulations. It does seem to me, however, that you might have a situation where, when a section of this kind is passed and the operation has to be worked out, you might need to give a considerable amount of discretion at the outset for operation by regulation; nevertheless you may reach the time when you have worked out a technique and do not need to go on in that way. I should like to know what the regulations are, to see whether that time has arrived, or whether it is perfectly clear that the regulations are still needed for operation. I do not wish to be sticky and to hold the thing up. Perhaps this might be left and dealt with later. I do not mean for the bill to stand, but-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand that in the case of this particular type of income the definition is complex. Under the old system it would read like this: "Such amount as the minister in his discretion may allow in respect of taxes on income for the year from mining or logging operations." That would have been the old system, because those are taxes which, if the provinces see fit to do so, they can continue to impose, although in some cases they turned over their taxation rights to the dominion. It is obvious that there must be some protection there for the dominion treasury. It is a concession that is being given. We would not have to allow this as a deduction if we did not want to do so, and nearly all these things are concessions to some taxpayer. The technique, for what it is worth, of regulation rather than ministerial discretion has been adopted, and in the larger act which will be before the house and the committee shortly, as those who examined Bill 454 last year will

Income War Tax Act
see, there are many cases in which provision is made for the adoption of regulations by the governor in council to cover what was previously handled by straight ministerial discretion.

I suggest to the minister that he has made a statement which may prove troublesome to him. I do not think the minister wished to say that it is a matter of concession, it should not be. It is a matter of equity, of justice, of balanced treatment between all concerned. I know the minister is capable of stating his own case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will not quarrel with my hon. friend about language, but it is permitting deductions from what would otherwise be income. It is allowing the taxpayer to deduct, from gross income at any rate, certain items which would otherwise not be allowed as deductions.
But it is not because the minister likes the taxpayer, or because of this or that accident. It is to do fundamental justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course. I do not quarrel for a moment with my hon. friend on that. He is absolutely right.

There is something else about which I am not clear. Is the reason why this cannot be stated definitely, the fact that the department is dealing with a situation which may change by reason of changes made by other jurisdictions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is because these taxes can be as varied as the colours of the leaves in the fall.
Perhaps the minister would explain that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures to impose any sort of tax they like on matters within their jurisdiction. We allow a deduction from future income tax for taxes on income for the year from mining or logging operations. One does not allow deduction of provincial income taxes on other types of operation, as my hon. friend knows. It is only in these special types of businesses. Ordinary provincial income taxes are not and never have been deductible from income for the purpose of dominion income taxes. That is the position. It is pointed out to me that in mining operations it is necessary to distinguish between milling profits, which is a form of industrial operation, and mining profits derived from getting mineral from the earth.

Is the minister saying then that if I wish to go
into this business or to set myself up in business, I am absolutely at large with regard to taxation? Is the minister saying that I do not know what my provincial tax will be or what my federal tax will be? Or have I misunderstood the minister? Is that what he said?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. If my hon. friend is in the logging business or the mining business, he knows exactly what his provincial taxation will be. But in order to determine how much of those provincial taxes, if any, he can deduct from his income in computing his federal income tax liability, he must look at the federal regulations. In the case of mining those may and do set out the rules to determine what portion of the profits are derived from milling operations in the case of a mine and what are derived from the mining operations. As my hon. friend knows, the reasons for allowing this deduction in the case of mining or logging operations are that those are the development of national resources within the provinces. They are the only two types of operations where income tax imposed by the province is deducted from income tax before federal taxes are computed. In no other type of business is that allowed.

I think the difficulty is that you call a royalty an income tax. It does not strike me that the wording is quite correct. It appears to me to be a kind of checkrein that the federal government has on our provincial governments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Royalties have always been deductible.

I think this must be a royalty. I cannot understand how we can pay a provincial income tax. What is the machinery to collect that? I know we used to have it, but actually I do not see any machinery for collecting it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ontario collects one, and has for years. It collects a tax on mining profits.
It does not single them out specifically, does it? These two businesses are not singled out specifically?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under their mining tax act, I am told they do.

At the risk of trying the patience of the minister, I intend to ask him to take a concrete example in either mining or lumbering, whichever industry he feels better able to deal with, because to some of us it is not quite clear what is the basis of the difficulty which makes the discretion so indispensable in these two cases.
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The regulations set out a formula as -to what constitutes mining profits as distinguished from milling profits. Some concerns operate mines and do not do any milling at all but ship all the ore to another smelter in order to have the minerals refined. Other mines combine the operations. Some formula must be determined for establishing what portion of the total profits of that second type of mine is true mining profits and what portion is profits derived from the operations of a smelter. I am told that is a fairly technical and complicated job. I know' that discussions have been going on for some time with the department of mines and resources of the various provinces, particularly I think with-

Quebec, Ontario and
British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -Ontario and British Columbia, to work out that formula. It is to put that in a formula that it is considered necessary to have this power of determining it by regulation. I think it is reasonable. It could have been by discretion. As I said before, it could be that the minister should allow as a deduction only such portion of the profits as he in his discretion might determine. But following the regulation principle which we are incorporating in the big act, and which I have discussed before, it was put in in this case as well. I think it applies particularly to mining companies, because I do not know that at the moment there is any specific income tax imposed upon logging operations. But it is perfectly open to any province to do so if it wants to, since in our offers to the provinces we have specifically said that income tax with respect to mining and logging operations may be deducted from income for purposes of computing dominion tax. I repeat what I said before, that it is only with respect to these two types of businesses that that special provision applies.

I can understand that there may be an arbitrary determination that mining and lumbering shall be subject to a tax, but until I have further information I have difficulty in distinguishing any ground for particular treatment of mining, let us say, as compared with wheat growing, other -than the aspect of depletion. I am not dealing with depletion at the moment, because that is dealt with in a particular way and according to arbitrary regulations which are applied. A mine brings up its ore, and the rough ore goes through a preliminary refinement which permits the unrefined metal to be shipped to the smelter. There is the mining operation;

there is the preliminary milling operation. The smelting is done elsewhere. If it is lead, it is done in Belgium or in one of the remote states of the union. We have no lead smelter in Canada at the present time. How does that differ from -the growing of wheat, leaving aside the matter of depletion? The wheat is grown on the land. It is a natural resource. It is mined. Later it is milled and refined. What is there in those two operations that is so entirely different as to make it necessary to enact particular rules in the one case, whereas general rules apply to the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There may be some similarity. One can grow another crop of wheat or crop after crop of wheat, but one cannot grow another crop of ore.	Once the mine is
exhausted, there is no more mine.
Another crop of timber can be grown.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is true that another timber crop can be grown if one follows a suitable reforestation policy, but it is a longterm matter. As my hon. friend knows, depletion is allowed in connection with timber limits and it is not allowed in connection with wheat fields. There is the general principle. It is probably not relevant to this discussion, but in the dominion-provincial discussions this provision was asked for by all the provinces, particularly by Quebec and Ontario where there are large mineral and lumber resources. It seems fair that in the case of taxes imposed with respect to these great natural resources of minerals and timber it should be allowed; and I think one province, Ontario, has urged that the royalty tax in these matters is an unfair and unsatisfactory method of collecting revenue from these resources. Ontario has urged that it should be in the nature of an income tax, and that a mine should not pay anything unless it was making a profit out of its operation. There is a good deal to be said for that point of view. A royalty is paid whether or not the mine is a profitable operation, whereas a form of income tax, because it is a tax on income, is payable only if the mine makes a profit. That was urged quite strongly, and that view has been recognized in permitting a deduction of what is an income tax from the dominion tax, in the case of these two types of natural resources.

I thought I understood this at one stage, but I have slipped back; and I am going to put part of the blame on the minister, rightly or wrongly.

Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These are complicated and technical matters. I do not wonder that my hon. friend is confused.

I may not understand it now, but I want to understand it; and I want to recall to the minister two things he said. At one time I asked if the need for this rather flexible arrangement resulted from the fact that he had to deal with unknown and perhaps unpredictable tax situations in other jurisdictions, and I think the minister said yes. Then I asked whether that meant anyone going into a business of this kind is at large with regard, first of all, to the provincial tax and, then, the dominion tax; and, as I understood him, the minister said, "Oh, no. Everybody knows what the provincial taxes are."
iMr. ABBOTT: If they do not they can find out.

But if that last statement stands, if I have stated it correctly, I am still in the difficulty mentioned by the hon. member for Stanstead, in failing to understand, why, if you know the conditions, if there is no unknown as far as your imposition of the tax or your relief from the tax is concerned, it has to be left discretionary. I am still perplexed about that, as to why you cannot state now what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, the provincial authorities may impose a tax on mining companies. They do that under the mining tax acts. They may do that instead of royalties, they impose what is in the nature of an income tax. As I understand it, that is a tax on all the income of the mining company including refining profits as well as mining profits. So the dominion government, in allowing a deduction from its own tax in this case, confirms by regulation a formula which we recognize for the purpose of determining the allocation as between mining profits and refining profits. The section must be made general because, if a province does not have such a law now, it may have one after the next session of the legislature. So we must have an enabling law here which will apply to all provinces; and that is what we have. I have not heard that there is any difficulty in working this out in practice. I am told it is workable, and I believe it to be. The regulations I have been referring to have been worked out as a result of discussions with the mining departments of the different provinces, particularly Ontario, and I am told they are
now in very satisfactory shape. I cannot say that from personal knowledge; I am only going by hearsay.

I am not complaining of
any dissatisfaction; I am trying to ascertain where the necessity arose from an understanding between the provinces and the dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told there was a great deal of discussion in working out the formula. That took quite a little time. There was a great deal of discussion with the officials of the provincial governments in working out a formula, and it may vary a bit, I am told, according to the different types of mining operations. But that is now completed, and I am informed that a reasonably satisfactory formula has been worked out and incorporated in these regulations, which were formally adopted about a month or so ago. One of the practical advantages of the regulation method is that if, in practice, defects are found in this formula, or if they find bugs in it, to use the colloquial phrase, it can be quickly changed.

There is one other aspect of the income tax act which applies to natural resources, about which I should like to ask the minister. I believe that in the United States the royalties accruing from owners' shares of oil stocks are free from taxation, and that here they are not. I understand that the minister's predecessor had some opportunity of discussing this matter, and I should like such enlightenment on the point as the minister may be able to give.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not that information available just at the moment. I did not know that in the United States the entire amount of royalties received was free from tax.
Only that portion which the owner gets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is referring to what are sometimes known as head royalties?
Yes, that portion which remains with the owner of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am surprised to hear that they are free of taxation, but certainly I shall look into the matter and see what the situation is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before this section carries, I should like to repeat our opposition to what the government has done under the provisions of paragraph (cc). As we have said previously, we wholly agree with the idea that assistance
Income War Tax Act

should be given to Canadians in advanced years. But we feel that if the government is going to give such assistance to the tune of an extra $5,000,000 a year it should have been done in some other way than by this provision. As the minister knows, this gives assistance to those who have sufficient income to be required to pay taxes, and the more taxes they pay, the greater will be their benefit. We feel that, instead, this $5,000,000 should have been given to those on old age pension. An alternative suggestion of considerable merit was made a few days ago in the editorial columns of the Ottawa Citizen, namely, that if the government wants to help people help themselves to a more comfortable old age, some of this money might well have been spent in lowering the rates of government annuities.

I want to ask one question on a matter which is of general interest in connection with the determination of income and the investigations that are carried on in arriving at that income. To what extent are safety deposit boxes searched without court orders? That is a matter on which there is considerable interest throughout the country, and I should like a statement from the minister. This is the first opportunity I have had to bring the matter to his attention in order to ascertain whether or not secret investigations do in fact take place without court orders and without notice to the taxpayers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Officials in front of me say they know of no case in which a safety deposit box has been investigated without a court order. I certainly know of none. Of course it is not in my department; it is in the Department of National Revenue. I have officials of that department in front of me, but they do not know of it.

I have a point to mention in connection with the determination of income. It concerns farmers' income. I would bring to the attention of the committee a situation which is quite general in Saskatchewan where the Minister of Agriculture on April 2, addressing a Liberal caucus-
-rapped political informers in income tax hounding.
I shall now read from a letter from a constituent which, if he wishes, I can send to the minister. The letter reveals a situation unfair to farmers. It states:
I made out my income tax forms. I totalled the whole crop that was threshed on the farm, including wheat, oats and barley; valued it at the market value, and stated the amount in the income column.

In other words, this man gave a complete and full statement. The letter continues:
Then I deducted all seed and feed which was fed and seeded on the farm, and showed that amount over in the expense column. Now I am told that I cannot be allowed because I actually did not buy the feed and seed.
Now, sir, that mistake has been made by numbers of farmers. The ruling of the department is that, because a farmer made a mistake such as that, there is no remedy. After all, we cannot expect farmers to be bookkeepers. I do not know many lawyers who can fill out their income tax returns with any degree of certainty. We have to go to the accountants to find out how to make out those returns.
And you have to check their figures.

I never got that far, because I never got my return back in sufficient time before I had to file it.
But here are farmers in Saskatchewan and elsewhere in western Canada who, because of their mistake in entering all their production, are being told that, having made that mistake, they have no recourse, and they must pay the full amount of the income tax. I point this out because it is the general condition. It is a complaint I have received from at least half a dozen farmers; and it is one which indicates a position under which officials rely too strongly upon the letter of the law, rather than upon the spirit of the law. I believe something should be done by the minister to tell officials that conduct of that kind can have but one result, andt that is the building of a feeling of oppression among the farmers affected. I hope the minister will do something about it. If a farmer is honest in making his return, and over-states his income by placing the total amount of his crop in the income column, then by reason of that mistake in bookkeeping he should not be denied the right to have his assessment made on a proper basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it would be most inequitable to omit it.
In other words, you force a man who has lost his wife to incur additional expense because he no longer has a wife. That seems to me a most extraordinary suggestion.

This provides that a married man who can afford to have a housekeeper the year round will have an exemption. I have a case in mind of a man whose wife was ill for six months. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I think in fairness I should make a brief explanation with respect to this section, and I hope I can get it through before eleven o'clock. Subsections 5 and 6 of section 9 are repealed. As I explained, and as is stated in the explanatory note to the bill, the present averaging provisions in the Income War Tax Act will be replaced by new provisions in the Income Tax Act which will shortly be considered by the house. However, in asking the house to repeal the present measures I should make a statement at the same time outlining the new provisions and explaining how they will differ from the present ones.
First of all, I might explain the reasons for making the change. They are twofold. The change is an attempt to meet the requests of farmers and farm organizations that the averaging should cover a period longer than the present three-year provision. The second purpose is to remove some of the complexities involved in fitting a moving average into a system which at the same time allows the carry backward and forward of losses.
It is proposed that the present three-year moving average be replaced by a five-year averaging on what might be called a "block system". Under the so-called "block system", a farmer may average income for a five-year period and follow it subsequently with a second five-year period, and so on. The averaging periods do not overlap under the block system as they do under the moving average introduced two years ago.
Under the proposed system, the farmer will continue to use the one-year carry back and three-year carry foward of losses. He will then be permitted to average on a five-year basis the incomes as they stand after adjustment for losses.
One of the objections to a period as long as five years was that a farmer would have to wait for this period before securing any benefits from it. It is proposed, therefore, that a farmer may at his option average at the end of four years in the first instance. Thus, the first period for which averaging may be adopted will be 1946, 1947, 1948 and 1949. In

the meantime the farmer will be able to take full advantage of the carry backward and forward of losses.
I believe the new system outlined retains all the benefits which could properly have been obtained under the moving average. In addition, and I regard this as perhaps the greatest advantage of the new system, the new system will be simple to understand and use. I am afraid that the present law providing for a moving average to operate in conjunction with the carry forward and backward of losses might have been too complex for successful operation.
I make that explanation now, because the new bill will contain a provision for the five-year average, and I felt that I should not repeal the existing sections in the present act without making that explanation.
